Accessibility statement Honesty is worth more than a claim of full compliance: what we have achieved is set out here, and so is what we have not. Commitment

What we undertake The statement was prepared and last reviewed on: 7 August 2026. The statement is based on a self-assessment. ÖkoTech-Home Kft. aims to make the okoth.hu website usable by everyone, whatever device or assistive technology they browse with. We align the site with WCAG 2.2 AA level requirements. This is the level the Hungarian regulation transposing the accessibility directives also takes as its basis. Status

What we have achieved Structure and navigation every page is built with semantic HTML: header, main content, footer, a real heading hierarchy a skip link to the main content (“Skip to content”) is the first element on every page the navigation can be traversed entirely by keyboard the breadcrumb shows the page's place in the structure on every sub-page the dropdown menus are built on native HTML elements and work without JavaScript Presentation text contrast meets the WCAG 2.2 AA requirement — at least 4.5:1 for normal text focus is visibly marked on every interactive element information is never carried by colour alone text can be enlarged in the browser without loss of content touch targets are at least 44×44 pixels we respect the `prefers-reduced-motion` setting: for anyone asking for reduced motion, the animations stop Content every meaningful image has a text alternative; decorative elements are hidden from assistive technology form fields have labels; error messages are text and are tied to the field dynamic feedback is announced through an `aria-live` region, so screen readers receive it too tables have headers and a summary the language is marked with a `lang` attribute Operation without JavaScript Every meaningful function of the site works without JavaScript. Home Emptying cost calculator Cost calculator Emptying cost calculator The cost of emptying differs from one settlement to the next, and it is rarely a single figure: a call-out charge, a per-cubic-metre emptying charge and, in many places, a minimum charge all appear on the bill. This calculator works out the annual cost from your own tariff — and shows how much you pay for a volume that is never taken away. Call-out charge Emptying charge HUF/m³ Minimum charge Let us work it out The settlement database→ What this page gives you

reszek.cim: What it shows — and what it does not
reszek.szoveg: What it shows — and what it does not Emptying is not our service and not our price. This calculator exists so that, from your own tariff, it is clear what this costs each year and what it turns on. What it shows The per-visit and annual charge from the tariff you enter What makes up the amount — item by item How much you pay for a volume that is not taken away How the unit rate changes if you empty less often, with a fuller tank Where we have got to in building the settlement tariff database What it cannot tell you It is not a price list: we do not know every settlement's tariff, and we will not invent one It does not replace the utility's quotation or the local authority's decree It does not tell you how often to empty — the sludge level decides that It does not calculate VAT: enter what appears on your bill It sends nothing anywhere — the calculation runs in your browser, with no data leaving it The formula

How it calculates Five steps, every one of which can be checked on paper. The calculator contains no hidden multiplier and no “rule of thumb” correction. 01 Chargeable volume. The charge is not always based on what is actually taken away. Where the minimum charge includes a given volume, the chargeable volume is the greater. 02 Base charge. The emptying charge multiplied by the chargeable volume — but at least the minimum charge. The minimum charge is a floor: where the volume-based amount is lower, the minimum charge takes its place. 03 Call-out charge. Once per visit, regardless of volume. Not a separate item with every provider — in that case enter zero, and it does not appear in the cost bar at all. 04 Further items. A distance-based charge (HUF/km multiplied by the kilometres to be travelled) and any other per-visit item on your bill. Both can be left out. 05 Annual cost. The per-visit charge multiplied by the number of visits a year. You supply the frequency — the calculator does not estimate it, because it depends on the sludge level and on use, not on the tariff. reszek.cim: How much has to be emptied depends on the technology
reszek.szoveg: How much has to be emptied depends on the technology This calculator takes the tariff apart — how much has to be removed, and how often, is decided by the system installed. With a sealed holding tank the whole of the wastewater is removed; with a septic tank system, the sludge; with an active biological unit the operating profile is different again. The solution pages set out what each means. Emptying and maintenance with a septic tank system · Comparing solution types Request a consultation The calculator's result is indicative: it calculates from the values you enter and does not constitute a quotation. Emptying is not an ÖkoTech-Home service — the charge is set by the utility with local jurisdiction and by the local authority, and it changes over time. For binding figures, turn to the utility or the local authority. The calculation runs in your browser: the values you enter do not reach a server unless you submit them through the data submission form. Frequently asked questions

reszek.cim: What we are asked most often
reszek.szoveg: What we are asked most often Why do you not state the emptying charge for my settlement? Because we do not know it. Collecting domestic wastewater not carried by mains is a public service: the charge is set by the utility and the local authority, separately for each settlement, and there is no public, consolidated register of it. And we will not publish an invented or “roughly this much” figure — that is worse than nothing, because a visitor would believe it. This is why the calculator asks for the charges, and why we collect them settlement by settlement. What does it mean that the minimum charge includes x m³? That in return for the minimum charge the provider undertakes to remove a given volume — and if you have less removed, you still pay for that much. Where this volume equals the tanker's capacity, you pay for the whole tanker even if a single cubic metre is taken. This is why “volume included in the minimum charge” is a separate field in the calculator: it can be anything from zero up to the tanker's capacity. What if there is no call-out charge? Then enter zero in the field. The call-out charge is not a separate item with every provider — with some it is built into the volume-based charge or the minimum charge. The calculator treats zero as a real value, and this slice then does not appear in the cost bar at all. Should I enter gross or net values? Whichever appears on your bill — the calculator does not compute VAT, it only adds and multiplies. On a household bill this is typically the gross figure. If you work with net charges, the result will be net too; but do not mix the two within one calculation. How do I find out my settlement's tariff?

reszek.cim: What we are asked most often (part 2)
reszek.szoveg: From three places: your latest emptying bill, the utility's price table, or the local authority's waste management or wastewater transport decree. If you have any of them, you can submit it through the form — and the next enquirer will see it on the map. How often does it need emptying? The calculator gives no answer to this, because it is not a question of tariffs: the sludge level governs, not the calendar, and the frequency is determined by the tank's size, the number of users and how intensively it is used. reszek.lap: Bespoke wastewater treatment where there is no mains sewer
reszek.cim: Collecting, settling or treating wastewater— the three are not the same thing
reszek.szoveg: Collecting, settling or treating wastewater— the three are not the same thing Several kinds of system can come into play on a property without a sewer, but they do not do the same job. 01 A sealed holding tank collects; it does not treat. It stores the wastewater until the next emptying; no treatment happens inside it and no treated water is produced — nothing leaves the system except by tanker. There is no biological process to maintain, so it is indifferent to whether the property is used evenly or only occasionally: after a long gap it works exactly as before. In return it needs regular emptying, at a frequency set by the tank's size and the actual water use — and the running cost follows from that. It matters that the tanker can reach the tank safely. Its place is where local conditions permit nothing to enter the ground at all, and no other solution is possible. 02 A septic tank treats anaerobically; treatment is completed in the soil. Solids settle in the tank while the breakdown of organic matter begins in an oxygen-free environment. Treatment does not finish here, though: a significant part of the process takes place in the drainage field, with the help of the soil's natural microorganisms. It therefore works efficiently only with a drainage field of adequate size, typically two to three times that of a biological treatment unit. It runs by gravity, without electricity; but depending on how intensively it is used it generally needs emptying every 1–3 years, and most manufacturers also prescribe dosing with a bacterial preparation to keep the biological processes going. It can be a good solution above all for properties used intermittently or at lower loads. 03 A biological treatment unit treats inside the unit itself.

reszek.lap: Bespoke wastewater treatment where there is no mains sewer
reszek.cim: Collecting, settling or treating wastewater— the three are not the same thing (part 2)
reszek.szoveg: Microorganisms living in the system break down the organic matter in the wastewater in the presence of air (oxygen); aeration gives them optimal living conditions, so treatment runs continuously and efficiently. The result is treated water suitable for infiltration and for reed-bed use. Operation needs electricity to run the aeration system — thanks to which the bacterial culture sustains itself naturally, so under normal operation no regular dosing with bacterial preparations is required. It is recommended above all for properties in permanent occupation, where the system can work most efficiently at an even load; an ordinary holiday or an absence of a few weeks is not a problem. At the end of the process treated water leaves the unit, suitable for reed-bed infiltration. The entire treatment process takes place in a single tank installed below ground, with no daily intervention. A.B. Clear, made in Esztergom, puts this principle to work at both domestic and institutional scale. A.B. Clear systems are available up to a capacity of 1–50 people; we determine the size a given property needs from its usage data. The treatment process 1 · The wastewater arrives — All the domestic wastewater the household produces enters the unit: both the blackwater from the toilet and the greywater from laundry, washing-up and washing. 2 · Biological treatment — The bacterial culture living in the unit breaks down the organic matter in the wastewater. Aerated and settling stages alternate, so alongside the organic load some of the nitrogen compounds are removed too. The culture is self-sustaining: it needs neither additives nor replenishment. 3 · Handling the sludge — The surplus sludge produced during treatment collects in a bag, dewatered and stabilised. The patented sludge-bag technology is what makes this possible. Emptying the bag is a simple operation, and the dried sludge can be composted. This is why A.B. Clear units need no tanker emptying. 4 · Discharging the treated water — The treated water returns to the environment through reed-bed infiltration. Patented sludge-bag technology The surplus sludge collects in the bag. Simple to lift out and seal. The bag's contents can be composted.

Average and peak load We do not size for the maximum, but we do not ignore the regular peak either. Sizing needs four figures: average, peak, duration and frequency. The right question

reszek.cim: It does not a maximum, hanot a regular
reszek.szoveg: It does not a maximum, hanot a regular It is not worth sizing the unit automatically for the largest number of people the property will ever hold. A larger system chosen for one or two big gatherings a year will be persistently underloaded on every other day — and that is an operating problem in its own right, not a safety margin. A regular or sustained peak load must not be ignored, however. Guests arriving every weekend mean something quite different from a family celebration twice a year. So sizing needs four figures, not one: the average, the size of the peak, its duration and its frequency. Two separate peaks

What must not be combined Hydraulic peak — a lot of water at once Morning showers, the washing machine and the dishwasher together A large volume arrives in a short time The risk: water passes through faster than it should The unit's throughput capacity is the constraint It appears within the day, varying even by the hour Organic peak — a lot of matter to break down Guests, more cooking, a holiday weekend The quantity of pollutant rises, not necessarily the water The risk: the biological stage cannot keep up with the breakdown The bacterial community takes time to adapt Measured in days, not hours Four typical situations

Which applies to you? 01 Occasional guests. A few times a year there are more people. This typically does not justify a larger unit — the systems handle a short period of excess load. 02 A regular weekend increase. Occupancy is higher every weekend, or nearly every weekend. This is already a sizing factor, because it is not an occasional spike but part of the use. 03 A lasting increase in occupancy. A family member moving in, a child being born, a parent coming home. This raises the average, so it belongs in the average, not the peak. 04 Sustained underloading. The system receives considerably less than its nominal load — a longer absence, family members moving out. An active biological system's bacterial community needs nutrient, so this too is a distinct operating state, not „less trouble”. Oversizing is a mistake too

reszek.cim: Why „better safe than sorry” does not work here
reszek.szoveg: Why „better safe than sorry” does not work here An active biological system works with a living bacterial community that needs an adequate nutrient load. If the system persistently receives considerably less than its nominal load, that does not spare it — it is a distinct operating state that has to be managed. So we do not recommend the „let us just buy bigger” logic. The right size is the one that average load well, and handles the regular peaks as well — not the one designed for the largest day of the year. Where the spread really is wide — with seasonal use, for instance — it is to be handled not by sizing but by the choice of operating mode and technology. Next step

reszek.cim: If there are long gaps too
reszek.szoveg: If there are long gaps too Seasonal use is a case of its own: not simply less wastewater but longer periods of zero load and a peak returning all at once. This is a question of technology as well as of capacity. Load and capacity Seasonal use Frequently asked questions

reszek.cim: What we are asked most often
reszek.szoveg: What we are asked most often There will be six of us at Christmas and four otherwise. Do we need a larger one? Typically not. A surplus of a few days occurring a few times a year counts as a short peak. If it recurs several times a month, however, it is part of the use and has to be allowed for in the sizing. How much extra load can the system take? We deliberately give no figure for this at present. Our current material carries two different values on two different timescales, and it is not documented what exactly they refer to — headcount, volume of water or organic load, which models, and at what outlet water quality. Until that is reconciled, publishing a number would mislead. What happens under sustained overloading? The biological stage cannot keep up with breaking down the incoming organic matter, the outlet water quality falls, and the soakaway takes a greater load too — which shortens its life. This is not a sudden failure but gradual degradation, which is why it is often noticed late. We are planning an extension. When should we say so? At the design stage. If it is known that the family or the accommodation business will grow within two or three years, we allow for it when choosing the capacity. Replacing a unit afterwards is considerably more expensive than allowing for the growth from the start.

Drainage field The commonest misunderstanding: a drainage field is not the same as the soakaway after a biological system. Here the soil does not merely take the water — it treats it. The most important difference

reszek.cim: The field is not a drain — it is treatment
reszek.szoveg: The field is not a drain — it is treatment With a septic tank system, the drainage field formed in the soil is part of the technology, not a drainage accessory. It is therefore not the same as the soakaway used after an active biological system. The process has two stages: in the septic tank, anaerobic — oxygen-free — pre-treatment takes place, while a significant part of the further aerobic process happens in the field, in the upper, aerated layer of the soil. Treatment therefore does not finish in the tank. This difference also explains the larger space requirement, and why the field's position cannot be treated as a freely movable accessory. It is no accident that the legislation calls this “a septic tank facility with a drainage field”. The process

What happens, step by step 01 The septic tank. The wastewater arrives, the solids settle, and anaerobic breakdown begins. The water leaving is pre-treated but not yet treated. 02 Distribution. The pre-treated water reaches the field evenly, through a distribution system. Distributing the load evenly is a condition of operation — if one section takes everything, it saturates quickly. 03 Aerobic treatment in the soil. Microorganisms living in the field's upper, aerated layer break the organic matter down further. That needs oxygen — which is why it is critical that the layer is not compacted and does not end up underwater. 04 Disposal into the soil. The treated water percolates into the deeper layers. From here the same conditions apply as for any other discharge into the ground. Two systems, two space requirements

Why is the field larger? The soakaway of an active biological system The water arrives already treated The soil's job: to receive The size is a function of volume and infiltration Typically a smaller area The position can be chosen, within limits A septic tank's drainage field The water arrives pre-treated but not treated The soil's job: to treat AND to receive The size depends on the load and on the soil's oxygen supply too Typically a larger area Its position is a technological given, not a matter of layout What cannot go over the field

reszek.cim: How the area is used afterwards
reszek.szoveg: How the area is used afterwards The field's operation turns on the soil being aerated. Anything that impairs that impairs the treatment performance — not only the drainage. 01 Paving, concreting, compaction 02 Vehicle traffic, parking, storage 03 Planting deep-rooted trees and shrubs 04 Directing rainwater onto it — the field takes an extra load 05 Placing a structure over the field or immediately beside it 06 Breaking into the area without knowing where the distribution runs Next step

reszek.cim: The field needs measured soil data too
reszek.szoveg: The field needs measured soil data too Sizing a drainage field needs the soil's measured capacity to accept water and the groundwater situation just as infiltration does — and here the soil's oxygen supply counts as well. Treated water disposal Percolation test Frequently asked questions

reszek.cim: What we are asked most often
reszek.szoveg: What we are asked most often Why does a septic tank system need more room? Because there a significant part of the treatment happens in the soil, not in the unit. The field does not drain, it treats — and that needs area, an aerated soil layer and time. With an active biological system the treatment has already happened in the unit, so the soakaway has less to do. Can the drainage field be moved if the space is needed? Not freely. The field's position and size are technological givens, and the distribution system is designed to them. Moving it is essentially building a new field — which is why its position has to be decided at the start of the project, together with the garden plans. What happens if the field saturates? The treatment efficiency falls, the water percolates away less readily, and damp can appear at the surface. The causes can include compaction, overloading, rainwater discharged into it and neglected maintenance. Putting it right typically means partly or wholly rebuilding the field. Can a garden be planted over it? Lawn and shallow-rooted planting, generally yes. Deep-rooted trees and shrubs, paving, compaction and vehicle traffic, no. If you are planning landscaping, it is worth saying so when the system is designed.

Gradient and pipe depth This is the plot datum that most often emerges only during construction — and that is the most expensive moment to deal with it. Four levels, and everything is settled. Why now, and not during construction

reszek.cim: Levels are the most expensive surprise
reszek.szoveg: Levels are the most expensive surprise The height of the wastewater pipe leaving the house determines how deep the unit's inlet can sit. The fall of the ground determines whether the wastewater, and later the treated water, can move by gravity can be conveyed, or whether a pumped solution is needed. This is the plot figure that most often emerges only during the works — and it is then the most expensive to deal with. A riser element, a pumping chamber or extra earthworks can all still be thought through at the design stage; standing at the edge of the pit, they cannot. The four levels

What has to be measured Each is relative to ground level. A simple levelling and a tape measure are enough. 01 Where the pipe leaves the house. On which side of the house, and exactly where, the wastewater pipe leaves. On a new build this is a design decision — worth deciding together with the siting. 02 The invert depth. Not the top of the pipe but its bottom: this determines the level the unit's inlet has to reach. It is the single most important number on this page. 03 The ground level at the tank's intended position. If it sits higher or lower than the ground beside the house, that directly changes the depth of installation. 04 The level at which the treated water is disposed of. If the soakaway sits higher than the unit's outlet, it will not work without a pump. On level ground this happens more often than one would think. A slope is neither good nor bad

It depends on the direction A favourable situation The ground falls from the house towards the soakaway The unit can be placed between the house and the soakaway, at an intermediate level Both gravity inflow and gravity outflow can be achieved No pumping station and no pump are needed Less earthwork, simpler construction Calls for a separate solution The soakaway sits higher than the unit's outlet The pipe leaves unusually deep relative to ground level The ground falls towards the house and the free area lies uphill Level ground, with insufficient fall to the soakaway A riser, a pumping chamber or pumped conveyance then comes into play

reszek.cim: The task differs for a new build and an existing house
reszek.szoveg: The task differs for a new build and an existing house On a new build the position and depth at which the pipe leaves can still be influenced. This is the cheapest moment: in consultation with the services engineer the outlet can be put where the unit fits too, and at a depth workable without a riser or a pumping station. It is worth going through the wastewater system before the construction drawings are finalised. On an existing house the pipe exit is a given, so it has to be measured. The most reliable way is to open up or find the existing chamber and measure the invert relative to ground level. If that cannot be done, it can form part of the on-site survey. The result

Four possible outcomes 01 A gravity arrangement is likely. The levels work out; it can be done without a pump or a riser. 02 A riser has to be examined. The unit would sit deeper than usual; a riser section may handle it, but the permitted extent has to be checked model by model. 03 A pumping station is likely. The depth, or the level of the soakaway, makes a pumped solution necessary. This affects both the capital cost and the operation. 04 On-site levelling is needed. The levels are not reliably known. Measurement settles this — it cannot be designed from an estimate. Next step

reszek.cim: Can the machine get in? And the service?
reszek.szoveg: Can the machine get in? And the service? After the levels comes access. Two separate questions: getting the machinery in for the installation, and lasting access to the system during operation. Plot suitability overview Vehicle loading and access Frequently asked questions

reszek.cim: What we are asked most often
reszek.szoveg: What we are asked most often What is the invert? The lowest point inside the pipe — where the water actually flows. For sizing, what counts is not the top of the pipe or the ground surface but this. That is why we always ask for the invert depth, relative to ground level. Is fall not a problem on a level plot? Not necessarily. It is on level ground that the unit's outlet most often ends up below the level of the soakaway, making a pump necessary. Level ground is not the same as trouble-free levels. How much more expensive is a pumped arrangement? We give no specific price here, because it depends on the unit, the lift required and the conditions on site. What is certainly true: a pumping station means capital cost, electricity consumption and one more mechanical component to maintain. On a new build it is therefore worth avoiding it through the levels. We are designing a new house. When does this have to be decided? Before the construction drawings are finalised. At that point the position and depth at which the wastewater pipe leaves can still be chosen freely, which is the cheapest way to make the system work without a riser or a pumping station.

Groundwater With high groundwater there are two separate questions: can the tank be installed, and can the treated water be disposed of. There is often a technical solution to the first — the second does not follow from it. Two separate questions

reszek.cim: The tank and the water are not the same problem
reszek.szoveg: The tank and the water are not the same problem With high groundwater two things have to be examined separately: whether the tank can be installed safely, and whether the treated water can be disposed of on the same site. The two are often conflated, though their solutions and their limits differ. Installing the tank is a structural question. Where groundwater is high, ÖkoTech uses a concrete basin around the plastic tank, which prevents it floating up. Up to a certain water level this is therefore manageable with a separate technical solution. Disposing of the water, by contrast, is not structural but a question of what the ground will accept and of what the law permits. Government Decree 147/2010 sets separate conditions for discharge into the geological medium in areas with high groundwater and in highly sensitive areas. That the tank can be placed therefore does not make infiltration appropriate. Which water level counts?

reszek.cim: Not today's — the highest seasonal one
reszek.szoveg: Not today's — the highest seasonal one The groundwater level can vary considerably over the year. A measurement at the end of summer may show the most favourable state, while in spring or after a long wet spell the water may stand metres higher. For sizing and for the installation decision, what counts is the the highest typical seasonal water level is what governs. In practice this means a single instantaneous measurement is rarely enough on its own. What is needed is either a longer period of observation, a document that includes the seasonal maximum, or an expert estimate from the local stratification. Sources of data

reszek.cim: How can the groundwater level be found out?
reszek.szoveg: How can the groundwater level be found out? Reliability increases from the bottom up. The first two serve for pre-screening; sizing needs the rest. 01 Experience from nearby. Water in a cellar, spring water levels in the garden, earlier excavation. Indicative, and often the only thing available at once. 02 Your own observation. The water level in a dug well, water breaking into an earlier pit, wet patches in the garden. Worth dating and photographing — here the date of the observation is worth at least as much as the observation itself. 03 Well documentation. For a drilled well it may contain the strata log and the rest water level. Take care whether it refers to groundwater or to deeper aquifer water — the two are not the same. 04 A geotechnical or hydrogeological report. This gives both measurement and interpretation. In an uncertain situation, in a highly sensitive area or near a water base protection zone, it is the only acceptable source. What groundwater affects

reszek.cim: The same figure, two separate consequences
reszek.szoveg: The same figure, two separate consequences On installing the tank Risk of flotation with an empty or partly filled tank Whether a concrete surround or another anchored arrangement is needed Dewatering the excavation during construction The stability of the pit, shoring Extra earthworks and extra cost The timing of installation — a drier period On disposing of the treated water The distance required between the soakaway and the groundwater The soil's actual capacity to accept water at a high water level The separate conditions under 147/2010 in areas with high groundwater Whether infiltration is permitted in a highly sensitive area Another route for water disposal, if one is needed Whether hydrogeological or regulatory review is needed The result

Four possible outcomes 01 Standard installation. The groundwater stays below the level of the tank and the soakaway even at its seasonal maximum. The usual arrangement is likely. 02 Separate anchoring of the tank or a riser has to be examined. The tank can be placed, but with a structural solution. This affects both the project's cost and its construction time. 03 Water disposal has to be examined separately. The tank can be dealt with, but the adequacy of infiltration is not established. A percolation test, or possibly another means of disposal, follows. 04 Expert or regulatory review is needed. In a highly sensitive area, near a water base protection zone, or with unknown stratification, a hydrogeologist or the authority decides. Next step

reszek.cim: A well on the plot is a separate question
reszek.szoveg: A well on the plot is a separate question The presence of a well does not rule the system out, but from a water protection standpoint the sealed tank and the soakaway are assessed separately. No single universal protective distance can be given — the next page shows what determines it. Plot suitability overview Wells and protective distance Frequently asked questions

reszek.cim: What we are asked most often
reszek.szoveg: What we are asked most often Water stands in the garden in spring. Does that mean high groundwater? A signal, but not proof. Water standing at the surface can come from an impermeable clay layer, poor surface drainage or compacted soil, not necessarily from the groundwater level. It is nonetheless exactly the kind of observation worth reporting — with a date and a photograph — because it warrants investigation. If the tank can be anchored, can the water be infiltrated too? Neither follows from the other. Anchoring is a structural solution against flotation. Whether infiltration is appropriate depends on whether the soil will accept the daily volume even at a high water level, and on whether the area's classification permits it. These are the two most important separate questions. I do not know the groundwater level. Does that rule the project out? No. That is a „to be examined” state, not a refusal. The figure can be obtained: from well documentation, an earlier expert report, observation or expert measurement. The pre-screener shows which route is shortest in your case. What does a highly sensitive area mean? The sensitivity classification of settlements with regard to subsurface water appears in an official register, and in the highly sensitive category stricter conditions apply to putting treated wastewater into the geological medium. The classification is amended from time to time, so it must always be checked against a current source.
Guesthouses and hospitality A twenty-bed guesthouse may run at eight guests on annual average and twenty on three peak weekends. The two figures call for different systems. Bed count is not load

reszek.cim: What it is really made of
reszek.szoveg: What it is really made of In sizing a guesthouse or a hospitality business, the nominal bed count is not the same as the treatment unit's actual load. A twenty-bed guesthouse may run at an annual average of eight guests with twenty on three peak weekends — the two call for quite different systems. Alongside bed spaces, the load profile therefore needs the annual occupancy rate, the peak periods, the opening hours, the staff, and the water use of the laundry, the wellness facilities and any catering. Two separate wastewater streams

reszek.cim: What it does not szabad egybevenni
reszek.szoveg: What it does not szabad egybevenni Domestic — the guests' wastewater Bathroom, WC, handbasin Its composition resembles household wastewater It varies in proportion to the occupancy rate With hydraulic peaks morning and evening This is the task of ordinary biological treatment Kitchen — the water used in catering Washing up, preparation, cleaning A higher organic, fat and oil load Proportional not to the number of guests but to the number of meals With short, intense peaks following the kitchen's hours It may need PRE-TREATMENT — a grease trap What you need to provide

The accommodation load profile 01 Bed count and average annual occupancy. Together the two give a realistic average; the bed count alone shows the maximum. 02 Peak periods. When it is full, for how long, and how many times a year. At a guesthouse on Lake Balaton this is a few weeks; in a city it follows events. 03 Days of opening. Open all year or seasonally. If seasonally, the seasonal use page is relevant too. 04 Number of staff. They too represent a load, typically for the whole of the opening hours. 05 Catering. Breakfast only, or a full restaurant. The number of meals a day and the kitchen's operating hours. 06 Laundry. Laundry done on site or by an outside service. An in-house laundry is a substantial, concentrated water use. 07 Wellness facilities. Pool, jacuzzi, sauna. Changing the pool water is a separate, large one-off volume. 08 Events. A wedding, a conference — a short, very large peak that does not come from the residential guests. The kitchen is a separate question

reszek.cim: It cannot be solved by “guests × litres”
reszek.szoveg: It cannot be solved by “guests × litres” The fat and oil load of catering wastewater differs from household wastewater, and it directly affects how the biological stage works. At higher kitchen loads the technology can be supplemented with a grease trap — but when that is needed has to be derived from the actual operation. For wastewater arising from production and service activities, Government Decree 220/2004 treats process and operating data as relevant inputs too. In practice this means a project with a commercial kitchen cannot be sized by a simple „covers × litres per head” method. Where the kitchen load is significant, the questions of laboratory data and pre-treatment enter early — worth reckoning with rather than meeting at the end of the project. Next step

reszek.cim: For institutions the logic differs again
reszek.szoveg: For institutions the logic differs again For a school, a nursery, an office or another community institution, what governs alongside the nominal headcount is the hours of attendance and the operating days per year. Load and capacity Institutional load Frequently asked questions

reszek.cim: What we are asked most often
reszek.szoveg: What we are asked most often My guesthouse has twenty beds. Do I need a twenty-person system? Not necessarily — probably not. The bed count shows the maximum, but sizing starts from the average occupancy and the regular peaks. Give us the annual occupancy and the number of peak weekends, and a considerably more accurate picture comes together from that. We have a restaurant too. What does that change? A great deal. The grease and organic load of kitchen wastewater differ from household effluent, and it may require pre-treatment — typically grease separation. Sizing needs the number of meals a day and the kitchen's operating hours, not the guest nights. We hold events as well. Should we size for those? An event is a short, very large peak, and it is typically not worth handling with the size of the unit — that would mean over-sizing on every other day of the year. Give us the frequency and the scale, and we will look at the right approach in that case. Is a laboratory analysis needed? At an accommodation business the domestic-type load can usually be estimated well. Where there is a significant kitchen or other process load as well, laboratory data is often unavoidable — without it the sizing would rest on assumption.

High groundwater situations High groundwater is not an automatic refusal. It breaks into two separate questions — and while the first usually has a structural solution, nothing about the second follows from it. Two separate problems

The tank and the water In high groundwater two things have to be examined separately: placing the tank safely in the ground, and whether the treated water leaving it can be disposed of. These are not the same, and neither follows from the other. The question of the tank is structural: where groundwater is high, ÖkoTech uses a concrete basin around the plastic tank, which prevents it floating up. Up to a certain water level this can therefore be solved. Disposing of the water, by contrast, is a question of what the ground will accept and what the law permits . In areas with high groundwater, Government Decree 147/2010 makes the use of an individual treatment facility subject to separate conditions, and in highly sensitive areas to the water base protection rules. That the tank can be anchored does not make infiltration appropriate. Which water level governs?

The seasonal maximum The groundwater level can vary by metres over the year. A measurement at the end of summer shows the most favourable state, while in spring or after a long wet spell the water may stand much higher. For the decision, what counts is the the highest typical seasonal water level is what governs. This means a single instantaneous measurement is rarely enough. What is needed is either a longer period of observation, a document that includes the seasonal maximum, or an expert assessment from the local stratification. Early signs

reszek.cim: What can point to high groundwater?
reszek.szoveg: What can point to high groundwater? These are signals, not proof — but every one of them warrants a test. It is worth recording them with a date and a photograph. 01 A damp or flooding cellar in the house or next door 02 A shallow water level in a dug well, measured from ground level 03 Water breaking into the pit during earlier excavation — footings, a pool 04 Water standing for long periods in the garden in spring or after rain 05 Reeds or sedges on the plot or immediately around it 06 Experience nearby: at whose property, and at what depth, the water rose The result

reszek.cim: Four separate branches — not an automatic refusal
reszek.szoveg: Four separate branches — not an automatic refusal 01 Anchoring the tank is needed. Installation can be achieved, but with a structural solution. That carries consequences for cost and for construction. 02 Water disposal has to be examined separately. The tank can be dealt with, but the adequacy of infiltration is not established. A percolation test and establishing the groundwater level follow. 03 Regulatory or hydrogeological review is needed. In a highly sensitive area, near a water base protection zone, or with unknown stratification, the supplier of the unit does not decide. 04 Another route for disposal is needed. Where on-site disposal cannot be substantiated, the project does not close — it takes another direction, and that needs a qualified designer. Next step

reszek.cim: The water level alone is not enough
reszek.szoveg: The water level alone is not enough Even in high groundwater it is the soil's measured capacity to take water that decides what can be built — the two have to be looked at together. Where the data is missing or the case is borderline, it is worth going straight to the expert route. Percolation test When you need an expert Frequently asked questions

reszek.cim: What we are asked most often
reszek.szoveg: What we are asked most often Can no system be installed at all where groundwater is high? That is not so. Up to a certain water level, installing the tank can be handled with a structural solution. What has to be examined separately is whether the treated water can be disposed of — and that is the harder question, because alongside the soil's capacity the area's classification counts too. Can the tank float up? In high groundwater this is a real risk, particularly with an empty or partly filled tank. That is exactly why we use a concrete surround or another anchored arrangement then. This is a design question; it cannot be solved afterwards. Is it enough to check the water level in summer? No. The state at the end of summer is typically the most favourable, and it says nothing about the spring maximum. If it can only be measured at one moment, that has to be recorded with its date, and the seasonal maximum estimated from another source — a document, observation or an expert.

To name a technical direction, however, we need the free area, the pipe exit level and at least an indicative soil and groundwater figure. Sizing needs measurement on top of those. Do I have to pay to obtain the data? Some of it is free or you already have it: title deed, building drawings, your own observations, photographs. reszek.cim: What we are asked most often
reszek.szoveg: What we are asked most often Where do I start if I know nothing yet? With plot suitability. The data examined there — soil, groundwater, free area, pipe level — determines most of the later decisions, and most of it can be obtained without calling anyone out. Do I have to request a quote for this? No. The pages in this section are written for orientation, and the pre-screeners ask for no contact details to use them. Requesting a quote makes sense once the questions of plot and load are settled.
Institutional load The 300 people do not use the facility all at once, all day, or all year. For sizing, the nominal headcount misleads on its own. The nominal headcount misleads

A „300-pupil” school is not 300 PE Describing an institution as „300-strong” is not enough for sizing on its own, because the 300 people do not necessarily use the facility all at once, all day, or all year. At a school the weekday morning-to-afternoon load, minimal weekend use, the school holidays and the commercial kitchen produce quite different hydraulic and biological states. The annual average conceals this, and the nominal headcount overstates it. Alongside the headcount, sizing therefore needs the hours of presence, the opening hours, the actual water use, the catering and the seasonal closure as well. The operating profile

What you need to provide 01 Type of institution. A school, a nursery, an office, a social care institution, a sports facility — their daily rhythms differ fundamentally. 02 Nominal and actual headcount. How many are on the register, and how many are typically present. 03 Hours of presence. How many hours they spend there. A nursery child present for four hours is not the same load as a resident. 04 Weekdays and weekends. Whether there is weekend use, and to what extent. 05 Operating days and holidays across the year. Summer closure, the winter break — these are long periods of underloading. 06 Actual water use. For an existing institution this is available, and it is considerably more accurate than any estimate. 07 Commercial kitchen. Whether there is a cooking kitchen, how many meals, and over what hours. 08 Sport, events, residential use. A gym with showers, evening events, a boarding house — each a separate window of load. Two different daily rhythms

An example of the difference A school without a commercial kitchen Load on weekdays between 8am and 4pm Close to zero at weekends and in the holidays Wastewater of typically domestic composition The peaks follow the breaks — waves repeating hour by hour With significant periods of underloading across the year A school with a cooking kitchen The same domestic load, plus the kitchen's The kitchen peak concentrates between 10am and 2pm A higher grease and organic load Pre-treatment — a grease trap — may become necessary The kitchen may run during the holidays too, if there is after-school care or a camp The band above 50 PE

reszek.cim: Where the question is no longer only capacity
reszek.szoveg: Where the question is no longer only capacity Above 50 PE the project is no longer in the simple standalone treatment category of Government Decree 147/2010. So alongside capacity, the permitting and the operating model become relevant early too. Sizing is then the task of a qualified designer, the questions of discharge requirements and monitoring enter, and operating responsibility is different too — not the owner's occasional attention but regular, documented operation. This does not make the project more complicated; it puts it on a different route. It is worth settling early, because the design and permitting lead times differ too. Next step

reszek.cim: If process wastewater is produced too
reszek.szoveg: If process wastewater is produced too If the institution or the site produces wastewater that is not purely domestic, the sizing follows a different logic: there the production technology and the laboratory data are the starting point. Load and capacity Special or industrial wastewater Frequently asked questions

reszek.cim: What we are asked most often
reszek.szoveg: What we are asked most often The school has 300 pupils. What system is needed? That single figure cannot settle it. It also takes the actual daily attendance, the hours spent there, the operating days per year, the holidays, and whether there is a production kitchen. At an existing institution the water consumption approximates all of this well — that is where to start. What happens over the summer holidays? A long period of underload arises, and it has to be managed. This is a question of operating mode and of choice of technology, and it counts in the sizing too: the system cannot be designed for the term-time load alone; it has to withstand the holiday state as well. Does the commercial kitchen count towards the headcount? That is not how to handle it. A kitchen load cannot simply be folded into population equivalent: its composition differs, its distribution over time differs, and it may require pre-treatment. It has to be given as separate data: the number of portions a day and the kitchen's operating hours. Who will operate the system? At institutional scale this is a question in its own right, not a side activity. At larger capacity, regular documented operation and typically monitoring are required too. It is worth deciding at the design stage whether this can be handled by your own staff or by a contractor.

Load and capacity The capacity required does not follow from the number of people. Water volume, organic load and the distribution of use over time decide it together — occupancy is only the opening question. The opening question

reszek.cim: “How many people?” is only the first question
reszek.szoveg: “How many people?” is only the first question The capacity a treatment unit needs does not follow simply from the number of people using the property. The volume of water, the organic load produced, and the distribution of use over time and the short or sustained peaks determine it together. At a family home the headcount can be a good approximation, and it is perfectly reasonable to start there. At a guesthouse, a school, a restaurant or a plant, however, the same number of „people” can mean quite a different volume of water and pollutant load — there the headcount misleads on its own. This section therefore offers no “Y unit for X people” table but leads to a load profile: the average, the peak, the peak's duration and frequency, and the uncertainties. From that the capacity range can be set on a sound basis. Two separate loads

reszek.cim: What has to be measured separately and sized separately
reszek.szoveg: What has to be measured separately and sized separately Hydraulic load — how much WATER arrives Average daily volume of water, m³/day or litres/day A peak arriving in a short time — morning showers, the washing machine Read from the water bill or the meter On a new build it has to be estimated This determines the unit's throughput capacity And it also gives the volume to be DISPOSED OF each day Organic load — how much MATTER has to be broken down The quantity of biologically degradable pollutant Its unit is the population equivalent (PE): 1 PE = 60 g BOD5 per day It cannot be read off the water meter It can be measured by laboratory analysis This determines the size of the biological stage High water use does not mean a proportionately high organic load The pages in this section

reszek.cim: Which situation is closest to yours?
reszek.szoveg: Which situation is closest to yours? It is worth starting with the concepts, then continuing with your own project type. Peak load applies to all of them. Population equivalent What PE means, why it is not the same as daily water use, and when occupancy will do instead. Population equivalent→ Occupancy and water use For a family home, occupancy is a good starting point — but the water bill is more accurate. How the two become usable data. Occupancy and use→ Average and peak load A short guest peak and sustained overloading are not the same. And underloading is an operating state of its own. Average and peak→ Seasonal use A long spell of zero load and a peak that returns suddenly. This is not only a question of capacity but of choosing a technology. Seasonal use→ Guesthouses and hospitality Bed spaces are not load. Occupancy rates, the kitchen, the laundry, events — and greasy kitchen water is a separate question. Guesthouses, hospitality→ Institutional load A “300-pupil” school is not 300 PE. Hours of presence, holidays, the kitchen, and the daily rhythm of the load. Institutions→ Special or industrial wastewater Fifty people working in a plant and a 50-person plant's process wastewater are not the same task. Industrial wastewater→ What to avoid

Four typical sizing mistakes All of them come from the same place: sizing from a single number. 01 Sizing to the maximum. If a few large family gatherings a year set the unit's size, the system is persistently underloaded on every other day of the year — and that is an operating problem in its own right. 02 Ignoring the regular peak. Twice a year is not the same as guests arriving every weekend. Frequency and duration count at least as much as the size of the peak. 03 Confusing water volume with organic load. High water use does not mean a proportionately high pollutant load — nor the reverse. In a restaurant it is precisely the latter that is the bottleneck. 04 Leaving out future expansion. If it is known that the family or the accommodation business will grow within two years, that has to be allowed for at the design stage. Replacing a unit afterwards is considerably more expensive. Next step

Start with the concept Population equivalent is the most commonly misunderstood concept in this field — and the misunderstanding leads to concrete sizing errors. A few minutes here, and every page that follows reads more clearly. Occupancy and water use Population equivalent Frequently asked questions

reszek.cim: What we are asked most often
reszek.szoveg: What we are asked most often Is it not enough to say how many of us live in the house? At a family home it is a good starting point, and often enough for a first direction. It becomes more accurate, though, if we also look at the actual water consumption on the bill and you tell us whether there is a regular guest peak or a planned change in occupancy. Why do we not size to the maximum occupancy? Because the bacterial community in an active biological system needs an adequate nutrient load. A persistently underloaded system is an operating problem in its own right — not a “safety margin”. The right approach is the average together with the realistically regular peak. What is BOD5? Biochemical oxygen demand over five days: the amount of oxygen the microorganisms in the wastewater use in five days to break down the organic matter. It is the measure of organic load — and the definition of the population equivalent rests on it. What changes above 50 people? The individual wastewater treatment category under Government Decree 147/2010 extends to a load of 1–50 PE. Above that the project follows a different regulatory and permitting route, and the design becomes an engineering task.

Load profile and capacity pre-qualifier It assembles a load profile; it does not calculate a price. It says whether a standard capacity range can be estimated, or whether measurement, laboratory work or an expert is needed. What it is, and what it is not

reszek.cim: A load profile, not a price calculator
reszek.szoveg: A load profile, not a price calculator From the usage data you enter, this module assembles a structured load profile and decides whether a standard capacity range can be estimated, or whether further measurement, laboratory analysis or an expert is needed. What it does not give you: a specific price, a guaranteed capacity from incomplete data, automatic industrial sizing, or a promise that the project can be permitted. The hard product and sizing rules come from an approved database. A generative model helps at most with structuring free text, bill data or an uploaded document — it does not invent the capacity required. How it runs

The project type comes first Because a usable profile is built from different questions for a family home, a holiday property, a guesthouse, an institution and an industrial project. 01 Residential. Permanent occupancy, water consumption, guest peak, absences, planned expansion. 02 Seasonal. The same, plus the months of use, the longest period of zero load and the peak on return. 03 Guesthouses, hospitality. Bed count, occupancy, season, catering, laundry, spa, events. 04 Institutions. Nominal and actual attendance, hours of attendance, opening hours, holidays, kitchen, water consumption. 05 Industrial or special. Technology, working pattern, m³/day, laboratory data, existing pre-treatment — here the module does not size but routes you to the expert branch. The output

What it flags separately Load data Hidraulikai average — napi volume of water Hydraulic peak — the volume arriving over a short period Organic load, where it can be estimated on a sound basis Short overload: its magnitude, duration and frequency Sustained overload, where present The length of underload periods Conclusion An estimated capacity range, where it rests on solid ground PE category, where the data allows one A list of the missing data Escalation to an expert, where warranted The above-50 PE route, where the load indicates it The need for laboratory work, where the wastewater is not domestic in character The possible outcomes

Four outcomes, four different routes 01 Standard residential capacity range. The data is sufficient and the load falls within the usual band. Design can proceed. 02 Borderline case — expert review. The load is near a category boundary, or the spread is unusually wide. Human review follows. 03 Above-50 PE route. The project leaves the standalone treatment category; it follows a different design and permitting route. 04 Special wastewater — laboratory and engineering analysis. The load is not domestic in character. Sampling and a feasibility study follow, not a capacity estimate. In the meantime

reszek.cim: What we are asked most often
reszek.szoveg: What we are asked most often Will I get a specific equipment model at the end? A capacity range yes, a specific model no. The final choice of model takes account of the plot's characteristics, the water disposal and the installation circumstances too — and those do not come from this module. Why does it give no price? Because the capital cost is not determined by capacity alone: the installation circumstances, the accessories required, the disposal arrangement and the earthworks all affect it. Estimating a price from capacity would mislead. Can the result be saved? Yes, the output is a saveable load brief: the profile, the estimated capacity range, the missing data and the recommended next step. It can be used directly for the plot suitability and technical discussions.
Occupancy and water use For a family home the number of occupants is a good first approximation — but actual water use is more accurate, and is usually available already. The practical starting point

reszek.cim: Occupancy is good — the water bill is better
reszek.szoveg: Occupancy is good — the water bill is better For a family home the number of occupants is a good first approximation to the capacity needed. A more precise decision, though, is helped by actual water use , because the same household of four can produce significantly different volumes. At an existing house it is therefore worth using the real monthly or annual consumption from the water bill or the meter. That is not an estimate but a measurement — and it is usually already available. On a new build there is nothing to read off, so an estimate from the occupancy, the expected way of life and the water-using appliances is needed. It can be refined later from the first year's consumption. Using the water bill

reszek.cim: How to turn it into a daily average
reszek.szoveg: How to turn it into a daily average A few minutes, and it yields a considerably more accurate figure than occupancy alone. 01 Take a full year. At least four quarterly or twelve monthly bills. A single month misleads: summer and winter consumption differ considerably. 02 Divide by 365. The annual cubic metres divided by 365 gives the average daily use in m³; multiplied by a thousand, in litres. 03 Deduct what will not become wastewater. Garden watering, filling the pool and watering livestock do not load the system. With a separate meter it is simple; without one it can be roughly estimated from the summer excess. 04 Look at the extremes. If one period is exceptionally high there may be a reason: a burst pipe, a leak or a one-off filling. Such a figure does not show actual use and has to be taken out. 05 Record the occupancy too. Dividing the daily average by the occupancy gives the specific consumption — this shows whether the household falls in the usual band or departs from it. Who counts, and how

reszek.cim: Four kinds of occupancy — do not mix them up
reszek.szoveg: Four kinds of occupancy — do not mix them up This is what to give The number of permanent occupants — those who live there day in, day out The typical number of daily users, where this differs Maximum occasional occupancy, together with its frequency A planned lasting change in occupancy — a child, a parent moving in Annual water use in m³, from the bill Flag these separately Garden watering or a pool — this will not become wastewater Equipment with high water use — a hot tub, several washing machines People working from home: more water use during the day Regular weekend guests, not occasional ones An earlier burst pipe or leak within the billed period What the water does not show

reszek.cim: The volume of water and the pollution are two separate figures
reszek.szoveg: The volume of water and the pollution are two separate figures High water consumption does not automatically mean a proportionally high organic load. Someone who showers and launders a great deal uses a lot of water, but their pollutant quantity does not grow in proportion — their wastewater is simply more dilute. The reverse also holds: a large organic load can arrive with relatively little water — typically where kitchen or process wastewater is also in the system. That is why we ask separately about unusual water use. In an ordinary household the two move together and the load can be approximated well from consumption — but with atypical use the two figures have to be handled separately. Next step

reszek.cim: The average is not yet the whole picture
reszek.szoveg: The average is not yet the whole picture Alongside the average daily load, when and by how much reality departs from it counts too. A guest peak, a longer absence and sustained overloading each carry a different risk. Load and capacity Average and peak load Frequently asked questions

reszek.cim: What we are asked most often
reszek.szoveg: What we are asked most often I do not have my water bill. What should I do? Consumption history can usually be looked up on the utility's customer portal. If that is not available either, an estimate can be made from occupancy and habits of use — just say that it is an estimate, because that matters for the sizing. We are building a new house and have no consumption yet. We then start from the occupancy and the intended way of life: how many people, how many bathrooms, whether anyone works from home, whether a pool or significant garden water use is planned. This is an estimate, so it is worth thinking through the headroom for expansion too. Does garden watering count? Not into the wastewater load: that water never reaches the system. It is in the water bill, though, so it has to be taken out. Without a separate meter it can be roughly estimated from the difference between summer and winter consumption. Our occupancy changes month by month. What should I write? Give the number of permanent residents, and separately the typical maximum with its frequency — „four of us live here, six every other weekend”, for instance. In the sizing it is exactly these two figures together that count.
Percolation test This measures directly what sizing needs to know: how quickly the soil absorbs water at the intended depth. Naming the soil is no substitute. Not a formality

reszek.cim: This is sizing's most important input
reszek.szoveg: This is sizing's most important input A percolation test is not an administrative step but the most important plot-specific input to sizing the soakaway. It measures directly what has to be known: how quickly the soil absorbs water at the intended depth. Naming the soil — sandy, clay, heavy — is no substitute. Two neighbouring plots may both be called sandy while behaving quite differently because of their layering. The test measures exactly that difference. The test

What to know about it 01 Where. At the soakaway's intended position, not at some arbitrary point on the plot. If the position is not yet decided, the layout has to be settled first. 02 At what depth. At the intended installation depth. A measurement near the surface may show something quite different from the layer a metre and a half below. 03 When. Preferably at a time when the soil is not saturated with rain — or the preceding weather has to be recorded with the measurement, because it affects the result. 04 Together with the groundwater. A good infiltration result is misleading without the groundwater: the seasonal maximum may reach the level of the soakaway, and the measured value then does not hold. 05 Documented. A home trial in a pit dug by a layperson and a professionally documented measurement do not carry the same weight of proof. Sizing needs the latter. What comes of the result?

Not a grade — an input The result of the test is not worth reading as „good” or „bad” soil. It is a number that, together with the daily volume to be disposed of, gives the infiltration area required — or shows that the area required will not fit and another means of disposal has to be found. Even a good result is not enough on its own: the groundwater, the available area, the proximity of a well and the area's sensitivity classification are conditions just the same. The test closes one question of several — but closes it for good. When it is worth carrying out

Timing When it makes sense Where on-site infiltration is the likely route Once the soakaway's intended position has taken shape Before buying a plot, where wastewater treatment is a risk factor If earlier soil data is old, or relates to a different spot Before anyone promises a specific soakaway size When to wait While it is not known where the house and the unit will go Where the mains sewer position is still unsettled Where the plot's water base protection situation is uncertain — let that emerge first Where the project's scale means engineering design will follow anyway Where a recent, documented measurement for the same position is available Next step

reszek.cim: If the result is not good enough
reszek.szoveg: If the result is not good enough A poor percolation result is not the end of the project. A larger area, a different arrangement or another means of disposal then comes into play — but the decision typically needs an expert. The next page shows who, in which case. Treated water disposal When you need an expert Frequently asked questions

reszek.cim: What we are asked most often
reszek.szoveg: What we are asked most often Can I do it myself? For orientation you can run a simple trial — filling a dug pit with water and measuring the fall — and it tells you a great deal. Sizing, though, needs a documented measurement carried out professionally: the depth, the water saturation, what went before and the method all affect the result. What does it cost? We give no specific price here, because it is a service and depends on the site and the depth tested. What is certain: considerably less than rebuilding an undersized soakaway afterwards. I already have a geotechnical report. Is that enough? It is often a good starting point, but two things have to be checked: which point of the plot and what depth it covers, and whether it contains any figure for the capacity to accept water. An investigation made for the foundations does not necessarily include an infiltration value. What if the result is poor? It means on-site disposal needs a larger area, a different arrangement, or possibly another direction. That is not a refusal but information — and far cheaper to learn now than after the soakaway is built.

Plot and water disposal pre-screener A pre-screening, not a certificate of suitability. It shows what looks like an obstacle, what is missing and what the next step is — without asking for contact details. What it is, and what it is not

reszek.cim: A pre-screening, not a certificate of suitability
reszek.szoveg: A pre-screening, not a certificate of suitability This module evaluates the plot data you enter against rules: it shows whether there is a visible technical or water-protection risk, which data is missing, and which next step is warranted. It asks for no contact details to use it. What it does not give you: a statement that the project can be permitted, a final product model, a specific price, or a guaranteed soakaway sizing without measurement. None of these can be settled from a form — they need an authority, a qualified designer, or a measured result. The module distinguishes a genuinely disqualifying condition from data that is simply missing. The two are not the same: the first is a property of the plot, the second of what you know — and only the first entails a restriction. The test menete

reszek.cim: In what order does it proceed?
reszek.szoveg: In what order does it proceed? It starts with the hard gates: if it stops there, working through the detailed questions is pointless. 01 Hard gates. Mains sewer position, the nature and scale of the project, the municipality's sensitivity classification, any known water base protection circumstance. A non-domestic or larger-capacity project is routed here to a separate expert branch. 02 Soil and water. Soil type, measured infiltration capacity, seasonal groundwater, wells and the intended disposal of the treated water. 03 Layout. Plot size, genuinely free area, pipe exit level, ground slope. 04 Access. Access, vehicle loading, service area. 05 Data quality. For each answer it is recorded separately whether it is estimated, known from a document or measured. This determines how much weight the result can bear. The result

reszek.cim: What it tells you, and what it does not
reszek.szoveg: What it tells you, and what it does not What it does tell you Whether a critical obstacle has been identified Which critical data is missing, and how it can be obtained Whether a separate technical element is likely — anchoring, a raised installation, a pumping station, a concrete chamber Whether the direction of water disposal is established, or still to be examined Whether an on-site survey is warranted, and what it would settle Whether hydrogeological or legal review is needed What it does not tell you Whether the project can be permitted Which specific equipment model will be the right one What it will cost The exact size of the soakaway, without measurement The payback or the running cost Anything within the remit of a qualified designer or an authority The possible outcomes

reszek.cim: Five outcomes, five different next steps
reszek.szoveg: Five outcomes, five different next steps 01 No visible obstacle. On the data known, the usual arrangement is likely. Design can proceed along the normal route. 02 Suitable with conditions. Feasible, but with a separate technical element. The result names the elements concerned. 03 Critical data missing. The constraint is not the plot but the information. The result says which figure, and where it can be obtained. 04 On-site survey warranted. Several uncertainties together, or a question that can only be settled on site. 05 Expert or regulatory investigation is needed. A water-protection, hydrogeological or legal question in which the supplier of the unit does not decide. In the meantime

reszek.cim: Let us talk about the actual plot
reszek.szoveg: Let us talk about the actual plot Until the pre-screener is running, we go through the same points in person. Write and tell us the name of the municipality, the size of the household and what you know about the plot — we will ask about the rest. If you have documents — a site plan, a section, a geotechnical report, a well data sheet — attach them: with those we reach a technical direction far more quickly. Plot suitability overview Get in touch Frequently asked questions

reszek.cim: What we are asked most often
reszek.szoveg: What we are asked most often Why does the pre-screener not give a clear yes or no? Because plot suitability involves several factors that can only be settled from measurement, official data or expert investigation. Without those a clear answer would rest on nothing — it would merely sound confident. Can the result be saved? Yes, the output is a saveable plot brief: what we know, what is missing, and the recommended next step. It can be passed on to the engineering colleague, to the on-site survey or to the designer. If the result is „not established”, is that the end? No. It means the intended solution cannot be supported on the circumstances known — typically because of the water disposal. Another means of disposal, another technology or an expert investigation then follows; the project is not closed.
Plot size and available area A large plot can be tight and a smaller one sufficient — the layout decides, not the square metres. There is therefore no universal minimum plot size. The wrong question

reszek.cim: The plot's size is not what governs
reszek.szoveg: The plot's size is not what governs The plot's total square metres are of little use on their own. What counts is the area genuinely usable: what remains once the house, outbuildings, the well, parking, trees, utilities and the intended garden functions are accounted for — and what will not be built on later either. Even a 1500 m² plot can be tight if the house stands in the middle, trees occupy the rear third, and what is left is the only access route. On a 600 m² plot, by contrast, there may be room enough if the layout is well planned. What needs room

Four separate space requirements These are not in the same place, and none substitutes for another. 01 The tank and the mechanical plant. The unit itself and the mechanical components that go with it. This needs the least space and usually causes the least trouble. 02 Disposal of the treated water. The area of the soakaway is a function of the daily volume of water and the measured infiltration capacity. It is typically a far larger area than the tank's — and it is what tends to be underestimated. 03 Access for servicing. The cover must remain openable and the unit inspectable and maintainable. Room enough for the tank to fit physically is not enough. 04 The space construction needs. Room for the machine to move, somewhere to put the excavated soil temporarily, and a route for lifting the tank in. This is temporary but indispensable on installation day. It differs by technology

reszek.cim: A septic tank system asks for more area
reszek.szoveg: A septic tank system asks for more area The space requirement is not the same for the two main solution types. With an active biological system the overwhelming part of the treatment happens inside the unit, and the soakaway serves above all to dispose of the water leaving it. With a septic tank system, by contrast, the drainage field formed in the soil is itself part of the technology: a significant share of the treatment takes place there. Its space requirement is therefore usually larger, and the field's position cannot be treated as a freely movable accessory. This is why one solution type may fit on a plot where the other does not — and the plot's size alone does not show it. Site plan

What to mark on it A hand-drawn sketch to scale does perfectly well. No designer's drawing is needed — it is the relationships that matter. 01 The outline of the house and where the wastewater pipe leaves it 02 Outbuildings, terrace, pool — both existing and planned 03 The position of the well or wells, including those on neighbouring plots 04 The driveway, parking, paved surfaces 05 The routes of known utilities — water, gas, electricity, telecoms 06 Large trees and planting to be retained, with the extent of the canopy 07 North, the plot boundaries and the direction of fall 08 Structures planned for later — the most commonly omitted item What cannot go over the soakaway

reszek.cim: How the area is used afterwards matters too
reszek.szoveg: How the area is used afterwards matters too The area over and around the soakaway cannot be used without limit. Compaction, paving, vehicle traffic and deep-rooted planting can all affect how it works. This has to be settled at the design stage, not when a pool or a parking space is to go in the same place two years later. This is why we ask about the later garden and building plans too. If it is known that a pool is going into the rear garden, the soakaway should not be designed there — even if that is the most convenient spot today. Next step

reszek.cim: The room is there — at what depth?
reszek.szoveg: The room is there — at what depth? After the horizontal layout come the levels: the depth of the pipe leaving the house and the slope of the ground determine whether the system can work by gravity or needs a pumping station. Plot suitability overview Gradient and pipe depth Frequently asked questions

reszek.cim: What we are asked most often
reszek.szoveg: What we are asked most often How large a plot does a domestic treatment unit need? We deliberately give no single figure, because it would not be true. The area needed depends on the solution type, the size of the household and the soil's measured infiltration capacity — the same plot is sufficient in one case and not in another. The layout governs, not the square metres. How far from the house does the tank have to be? The 2–10 metre distance is a manufacturer's and operating recommendation, not a statutory protective distance. The actual siting is determined together by the pipe exit level, the slope, access for servicing and the plot's characteristics. Can a terrace or a pool be built over the soakaway later? It is generally inadvisable and in some cases not permissible: compaction and paving impair the operation. If you have such a plan, say so at the design stage — the soakaway can then be placed elsewhere from the start. Is there any chance on a small, built-up plot? In many cases yes, but that is where the layout and the measured infiltration capacity really count. On a small plot the bottleneck is often disposing of the treated water, not the tank. It is worth drawing a site plan early in such cases.
Plot suitability overview This is not a detailed guide but a map: what has to be examined, in what order, and where it leads next. The detail lives on the individual pages. What this page is for

reszek.cim: A map, not a detailed guide
reszek.szoveg: A map, not a detailed guide This page runs briefly through the questions that have to be answered before the siting of a system and a direction for water disposal can be recommended responsibly. Under each topic it says only why it matters, what you need to know about it, and where you can go next. The detail lives on the individual pages. The order is not accidental. The first question is the mains sewer position and the plot's territorial classification, because a legal or water-protection circumstance can affect whether a standalone system is in play at all, before any technical detail. The test sorrendje

What is worth settling first? If your time is limited, work through them in this order: the earlier points determine what the later ones even mean. 01 Mains sewer and the legal starting position. Whether a mains sewer is available, and what the municipality's sensitivity classification is.
