If the plot lies in a designated water base protection zone, that affects everything else. 02 Soil and actual infiltration capacity. Not the name of the soil but the measured capacity to take water. This determines whether the treated water can be disposed of on site, and over how large an area. 03 Groundwater. The highest water level that occurs seasonally. It bears on installing the tank and on infiltration separately. 04 Wells and other water protection features. The position, type and use of your own and neighbouring wells. A sealed holding tank and a soakaway are judged separately here. 05 Genuinely free area. What remains once the house, outbuildings, driveway, utilities and trees are accounted for — and what will not be built on later either. 06 Pipe exit level and ground slope. The level of the pipe from the house determines the unit's inlet level; the slope determines whether the water can be conveyed by gravity. 07 Vehicle loading and access. Access for the installation, and lasting access for servicing. This is what emerges latest if it is not looked at in good time. Data quality

reszek.cim: Which figures may be estimated, and which have to be measured?
reszek.szoveg: Which figures may be estimated, and which have to be measured? Typically sufficient from a document or the owner's knowledge Address, land registry number, plot size — title deed, map extract Mains sewer position — water utility, local authority The position of the house and the free area — site plan Direction of the ground slope — site walk, photo Position and use of the well — site walk Access width, route for machinery — on-site measurement, photo Future garden and building plans — you know these This requires measurement or a documented investigation The actual infiltration capacity of the soil — percolation test Geotechnical stratification — expert report The seasonally highest groundwater level — measurement or an expert report The exact invert depth of the pipe exit — drawings or levelling Water base protection classification — official source Depth of the well and its aquifer conditions — well documentation Whether infiltration is permitted in a highly sensitive area — the authority What changes the design, and what stops it

reszek.cim: Not every problem carries the same weight
reszek.szoveg: Not every problem carries the same weight Some plot conditions only affect the design changes it: a structural solution for higher groundwater, a pumping station for a deep pipe exit, a concrete chamber for vehicle loading, a larger infiltration area for poorer percolation. These mean cost and construction time, not exclusion. Others, however, a separate expert requires it: an uncertain or designated water base protection situation, a highly sensitive area, unknown stratification, a plan to discharge to a surface receiving water. In these it is not the manufacturer of the unit that decides but a hydrogeologist, a qualified designer or the authority. That separation is exactly what this overview is for: before anyone quotes, it should be visible which category the plot falls into. Next step

reszek.cim: Start with the figure that determines the most
reszek.szoveg: Start with the figure that determines the most The actual infiltration capacity of the soil and the seasonal groundwater level are the two figures that determine most of the others. If you can obtain only one, start with these. Back to the plot suitability overview Soil and infiltration capacity Frequently asked questions

reszek.cim: What we are asked most often
reszek.szoveg: What we are asked most often How far do these figures get me before I request a quote? The pre-screener tells you whether there is a visible technical or water-protection risk and what is still missing. It gives no price, no final model and no statement that a permit can be obtained — those need a person and more data. What is the sensitivity classification? The sensitivity classification of municipalities with regard to subsurface water appears in an official register, and it affects the conditions under which treated wastewater may be disposed of into the geological medium. The classification changes from time to time, so it always has to be checked from a current source.

Plot suitability The tank will almost always fit somewhere. The system only works, though, if the treated water also has somewhere to go — and that is the harder question. Here we go through what decides it. What this section decides

reszek.cim: Plot suitability is not a single figure
reszek.szoveg: Plot suitability is not a single figure The plot suitability of a wastewater system is not the answer to a single question. The soil, the groundwater, the available area, the level of the wastewater pipe leaving the house, the terrain, wells and other sensitive objects, and the possibility of disposing of the treated water together determine what can be built on the plot — and in what arrangement. Government Decree 147/2010 itself requires septic tank and individual biological systems to be sized taking account of the soil's conditions, the depth of the subsurface water and the volume of wastewater. Further conditions apply in areas with high groundwater and in highly sensitive areas. Knowing a single figure is therefore not enough. This section recommends no product. Its purpose is to walk you through the critical plot conditions, show where each figure can be obtained, and let you see at the end where you stand: whether the data you have is enough for a pre-screening, or whether measurement or expert investigation is needed. Two separate decisions

reszek.cim: The tank will fit — the water also needs somewhere to go
reszek.szoveg: The tank will fit — the water also needs somewhere to go Whether the tank can be installed The physical placement of the unit on the plot Enough room for the tank and the mechanical plant The relationship between the wastewater pipe level and the receiving level A separate structural solution where there is groundwater — anchoring, a concrete basin Machine access and lifting the tank in Later access for servicing Disposal of the treated water Where the volume leaving each day goes The soil's MEASURED capacity to accept water, not its name The highest seasonal groundwater level The space the soakaway needs, as a function of the load Wells, water base protection, area sensitivity classification Where infiltration into the ground is unsuitable: another route for disposal Why this distinction matters

reszek.cim: The second question is the harder one
reszek.szoveg: The second question is the harder one The most common misunderstanding is to treat the two questions as one. That the tank can be anchored safely even in higher groundwater — ÖkoTech uses a concrete basin around the plastic tank in such cases — does not mean that infiltrating the treated water into the ground is also appropriate on the same plot. Water disposal is itself two questions: technically possible (will the soil accept the daily volume), and whether it is permissible in law and from an environmental standpoint can be applied at that particular place. Any of them can stop or change the project. The practical consequence: if the route for water disposal is unsettled, the project is not ready for a quote — even where the tank's position is already fixed. The factors to examine

What determines a plot's suitability? Seven topics, each on its own page. The order is not compulsory, but it has a logic: soil and groundwater affect most of what follows, while access is what emerges last if it is not looked at in time. Soil and infiltration capacity The name of the soil — sandy, clay — is not a sizing figure in itself. The question is how quickly the soil on site can accept water. Soil and infiltration→ Groundwater It is not today's water level that counts but the highest that occurs seasonally. Anchoring the tank and infiltration are two separate questions. Groundwater→ Wells and protective distance From a water protection standpoint, the sealed tank and the point where water actually enters the ground are not the same object. Wells and protection→ Plot size and available area The question is not the plot's square metres but the area genuinely usable once the house, the well, the driveway and the utilities are accounted for. Plot size→ Gradient and pipe depth The height of the pipe leaving the house determines how deep the unit's inlet can sit — and whether a pumping station is needed. Gradient and pipe depth→ Vehicle loading and access Vehicles cannot pass over the tank without a separate arrangement, and the system must remain accessible later. Loading and access→ How do I gather the data? Source by source: where it can be obtained, who can supply it, and which of them an estimate will not do for. Gathering data→ Four possible states

It does not „alkalmas" or „not alkalmas" Plot suitability is rarely binary. At the end of the examination the plot falls into one of these — and each carries a different next step. 01 Standard. On the data known there is no identified critical obstacle, and the usual arrangement is likely. This is neither a permit nor a final sizing — the design can proceed in the usual way. 02 Conditional. The installation is feasible but a separate technical element is needed: anchoring the tank, a riser, a pumping station, a concrete chamber or a larger soakaway. These affect the project's cost and construction time too. 03 To be examined. One or more critical figures are missing, or only an estimate is available. Here the problem is not the plot but the data: measurement, a document or an on-site survey closes it. 04 Not currently evidenced. On the circumstances known, the intended solution cannot be supported — typically for water protection or groundwater reasons. Another means of disposal, another technology or an expert investigation then follows. Next step

reszek.cim: Let us see where you stand with the plot
reszek.szoveg: Let us see where you stand with the plot If you do not yet know which data has to be settled, start with the overview: a short map of what to examine and in what order. If you already have data, the pre-screener goes through it, tells you what is missing and which next step is warranted. It asks for no contact details to use, and gives no statement on whether a permit can be obtained. Plot and water disposal pre-screener Plot suitability overview Frequently asked questions

reszek.cim: What we are asked most often
reszek.szoveg: What we are asked most often Is it enough for me to give the plot data, or do you have to come out? That depends on which figures you know and in what quality. If the critical ones — soil, groundwater, free area, pipe exit level — are known from documents or measurement, a remote pre-screening is often enough. If some of them are only estimates, a survey is not a formality but the only way to settle them. We say so separately under each topic. What if I simply do not know one of the figures? „I do not know” is a valid answer and means no exclusion. A route to obtaining the data follows from it: we say where it can be found, who can provide it, and whether a document will do or measurement is needed. Is a neighbour's experience acceptable as data? Useful as an early indication — particularly about seasonal groundwater — but not of equal weight to a measurement or an official document. In the pre-screening we mark separately whether a figure is estimated, documented or measured, because what comes next depends on it. Does high groundwater rule the system out from the start? No. It breaks into two separate questions: installing the tank safely, and whether the treated water can be disposed of. There is often a technical solution to the first. The second, though, depends not only on the groundwater but on water protection and area classification, and may require a separate examination. Does the pre-screening give you a permit or an official certificate? No. Pre-screening is technical orientation: it shows what looks like an obstacle and what data is missing. An authority rules on whether a permit can be obtained, a qualified designer on sizing, and a specialist on hydrogeological questions.
Population equivalent The most commonly misunderstood concept in this field — and the misunderstanding leads to concrete sizing errors. A PE is not a person, and it is not litres. The definition

reszek.cim: A PE is not a person, and it is not litres
reszek.szoveg: A PE is not a person, and it is not litres The population equivalent (PE) is the standardised unit for the biologically degradable organic load of wastewater. On the official European definition, 1 PE is an organic, biologically degradable load whose five-day biochemical oxygen demand — BOD5 — corresponds to 60 grams of oxygen per day. Two things follow. One: a PE is not a person but a load. Two: a PE is not a volume of water — not litres, not cubic metres. In Hungarian regulation the concept of standalone treatment extends from a load of at least 1 to at most 50 PE, so the PE is not merely a technical figure: it also determines the project's regulatory category. A correction

reszek.cim: The claim “1 PE = 135 litres per person per day” is wrong
reszek.szoveg: The claim “1 PE = 135 litres per person per day” is wrong ÖkoTech's current material says in one place that “1 population equivalent means a water use of 135 litres per person per day”. We correct that: it is not the definition of a PE. The figure of 135 litres per person per day may be usable as one's own hydraulic design assumption — an assumption about how much water is produced per person per day — but the population equivalent remains, independently of that, the unit of organic load. Keeping the two apart is not hair-splitting. A restaurant's daily water consumption and organic load stand in quite a different relation to one another than a family home's — take them as the same thing and the sizing will be wrong. The two concepts

When to use which PE — organic load Its unit: 60 g BOD5 per day = 1 PE The basis for sizing the biological stage Measurable by laboratory analysis It also determines the legal category (1–50 PE) For institutions and plants this is what governs From measured data: the daily BOD5 load divided by 60 g/day l/person/day — a hydraulic assumption Its unit: litres per day, per person A basis for planning the volume of water It can be approximated from the water bill A design assumption, not a legal category A practical starting point for a family home It also gives the volume to be disposed of each day When is occupancy enough?

And when it is not The approximation is the more accurate the more ordinary and domestic the water use is. 01 A family home, permanently occupied. Here 1 person ≈ 1 PE is a reasonable approximation, because the composition of domestic wastewater is broadly uniform. It is worth starting from occupancy. 02 A holiday home, a seasonal property. Headcount is still a good starting point, but how use is spread over time counts at least as much. 03 A guesthouse, accommodation. Bed count is not the same as load: occupancy, the laundry and the kitchen are separate items. Here headcount is only an entry figure. 04 A school, an office, an institution. The nominal headcount does not mean all-day presence. Without the hours of attendance and the operating days per year, the number misleads. 05 A restaurant, a plant, process wastewater. Here headcount is of no real use: the organic load arises from the activity, and laboratory data is needed for it. Next step

reszek.cim: In practice we start from the water bill
reszek.szoveg: In practice we start from the water bill Once the concept is clear, the actual figures follow. At an existing house the water bill is the most reliable starting point; on a new build, an estimate — the next page shows how these become usable load data. Load and capacity Occupancy and water use Frequently asked questions

reszek.cim: What we are asked most often
reszek.szoveg: What we are asked most often Do I need to know what PE is? On a family-home project not necessarily — there the headcount and the water consumption suffice. It becomes important with a guesthouse, an institution or a larger project, because there headcount no longer describes the real load, and the legal category depends on the PE too. How is PE calculated from measurement? Where there is a laboratory analysis, the daily BOD5 load is divided by 60 g/day. That requires knowing the daily wastewater volume and the measured BOD5 concentration. Without measurement it can be estimated, but an estimate it remains. Why does the 50 PE threshold matter? Because the legal category of individual wastewater treatment extends this far. Above it, the project follows a different regulatory route with different permitting and operating requirements — and the design becomes the task of a qualified designer.
Reed bed disposal The term covers several things in the market, so here we say exactly what we use it for — and what we do not. The limits on use matter as much as the possibility. What we mean by it

reszek.cim: The term has to be settled first
reszek.szoveg: The term has to be settled first The term “reed bed disposal” covers several things in the Hungarian market, so here we say exactly what we use it for: placing biologically treated water below ground on a planted area, where the water reaches the depth of the plants' root zone. So this is not surface irrigation, not a watering system, and not storing the water for later use. The point of subsurface discharge is precisely that there is no direct contact with the water. What we do not claim

reszek.cim: Three separate categories that must not be conflated
reszek.szoveg: Three separate categories that must not be conflated Below-ground disposal on an area of ornamental planting. This is what this page is about. Technically it is a variant of infiltration, with the addition that the water also benefits the planting. Indoor reuse. Toilet flushing or other household use requires further treatment. Biologically treated water is not suitable for that on its own, and it is unfit for human consumption in any circumstances. Regulated agricultural water reuse. This is a separate legal category: EU Regulation 2020/741 establishes its own water quality, monitoring and risk management regime for reuse within its scope. It is not to be confused with below-ground disposal in a domestic garden. Limits on use

What to watch for These are not undue caution: treated water is not of drinking water quality, and the manner of use determines the risk. 01 Below-ground delivery. The aim is that there should be no direct contact with the water — human or animal. Surface watering, spraying or the creation of aerosols is neither intended nor recommended. 02 Ornamental planting, not food crops. Watering edible plants is judged considerably more strictly and is not advised without a separate expert opinion. 03 Parts of the garden used by children. A play area, a sandpit, the surroundings of a pool — the point of disposal is worth planning further away here. 04 No storage. Storing treated water degrades its quality and adds risk; the system is designed for continuous disposal, not for collection. 05 It runs in winter too. Water is produced in winter as well, whereas the planting's demand for it is not. The system has to handle the winter too — which is why this is not “irrigation” but disposal. 06 Saturated soil. In wet periods the soil's capacity to accept water falls. The sizing has to withstand that too. No promises in place of evidence

What is genuinely convincing This counts as evidence A completed ÖkoTech project with photographs and a section drawing An accredited laboratory result for the water leaving the unit A technical drawing of the actual disposal arrangement Experience from a system running for several years Clearly stated limits on use This is not evidence A general claim of the “your garden will look better for it” kind The word “reusable” with no water quality data behind it A reference to another manufacturer's marketing Carrying the rules of agricultural reuse over to a domestic garden The phrase “reed bed irrigation” with no actual arrangement behind it Next step

A plot-specific discussion The conditions for a reed bed arrangement differ from plot to plot: the soil, the groundwater, the planting and the use of the garden decide together. Write and tell us what you are planning in the garden and we will say what of it can be built. Treated water disposal Get in touch Frequently asked questions

reszek.cim: What we are asked most often
reszek.szoveg: What we are asked most often Is the treated water drinkable? No. It is not fit for human consumption under any circumstances, and we do not treat it towards that end. Biological treatment reduces the pollutant load; it does not produce drinking water. Can I water vegetables or fruit with it? We do not advise watering food crops without a separate expert opinion. It is judged considerably more strictly than ornamental planting, and regulated agricultural water reuse is a separate legal category besides. Can I use it for flushing the toilet? Not without further treatment. Indoor reuse is a technological question in its own right, with its own equipment and conditions — not simply piping the treatment unit's output indoors. What happens in winter? Wastewater is produced in winter too, while the planting's demand for water is minimal. The system is therefore designed not for irrigation but for continuous disposal: the soil has to receive the winter period as well. The sizing has to withstand that. Is this the same as reed bed treatment? No. A reed bed system is a treatment technology in its own right. What is discussed here is the disposal of already treated water on a planted area — a different function, despite the similar name.
Seasonal use A seasonal load does not mean less wastewater but long breaks and peaks that return all at once. This is not only a question of capacity. Not simply less

reszek.cim: A long gap, a sudden peak
reszek.szoveg: A long gap, a sudden peak A seasonal load does not mean „less wastewater”. It means longer low or zero periods of load alternate with peaks that return suddenly — and the two together are a different task from continuous, even use. An active biological system works with a living bacterial community that needs a continuous supply of organic matter. After a long break that community shrinks, and it cannot handle the returning load straight away. Seasonal use is therefore not only a question of capacity, hanot choosing a technology but of : for certain usage profiles a passive septic tank system may be the more relevant one. The load profile

What to record Calculating an annual average occupancy is not worth doing here — it conceals precisely what matters. 01 Months of use. In which months the property is used at all. 02 The pattern of use. Every weekend, only in the summer season, or sporadically. 03 The length of the peak season and the numbers. For how many weeks and with how many people. 04 The longest spell of zero load. This is the single most important figure on this page — the operating mode or shutdown procedure required depends on it. 05 The peak on return. Whether full load arrives immediately after the break, or use builds up gradually. 06 Power supply during absence. Whether the unit stays powered when no one is there. Two operating states

reszek.cim: A short and a long absence — not the same thing
reszek.szoveg: A short and a long absence — not the same thing A shorter gap — weekend-house use The unit stays in operation An underload mode, where the controls support it The bacterial community survives Returning needs no separate intervention The power supply has to be continuous A long gap of several months Shutting the unit down may come into play Emptying and refilling with clean water Recommissioning is needed in spring The biology takes time to restart This is a planned procedure, not „we just switch it off” Choosing a technology

reszek.cim: When the pattern of use decides, not the size
reszek.szoveg: When the pattern of use decides, not the size If use is strongly intermittent — a summer-only holiday home with a long winter gap, for instance — the question is no longer „what size of system is needed” but which technology takes that pattern well. An active biological system is built for continuous operation and handles a long break with a separate procedure. The passive septic tank system is more tolerant in this respect, because it does not rest on continuously sustaining a living, active sludge community. This does not mean an active system is unsuited to a holiday home — it means the usage profile has to be looked at when choosing, not just the headcount. Next step

reszek.cim: If you take guests as well
reszek.szoveg: If you take guests as well If the property is not only used by the family but also runs as accommodation, the load comes together on a different logic: bed count, occupancy and any catering, together. Load and capacity Guesthouses and hospitality Frequently asked questions

reszek.cim: What we are asked most often
reszek.szoveg: What we are asked most often We do not use the holiday home in winter. What happens to the system? A gap of several months calls for a planned procedure — typically shutdown, emptying, refilling with clean water, then recommissioning in spring. The exact time limits and steps are set out in the unit's current user guide, so this always has to be settled for the specific model. Is an active biological system right for a weekend house? With regular weekend use, yes, provided the controls support an underload mode and the unit stays powered. Where use is more intermittent than that — with long gaps of several months — the passive system is worth examining too. Does it need electricity while we are away? With an active biological system, yes: aeration is needed to sustain the bacterial community, and it runs during absences too, in reduced mode. If the property has no electricity over the winter, that has to be flagged in advance when choosing the technology. How long does the system take to restart in spring? Restarting the biology takes time — the outlet water quality does not reach its usual level from the first day. We publish no specific duration here, because it depends on the model, the temperature and the load; the commissioning documentation records it.

Soakaway infiltration Biological treatment has already happened inside the unit — the soakaway's job is to dispose of the water leaving it. Sizing turns on the daily volume and on the soil's MEASURED capacity to accept water. What it means

Disposing of water already treated With an active biological system, infiltration is not the main process of treatmentbut the placing of already biologically treated water into the soil. The distinction matters: here the soakaway does not treat, it receives. The arrangement is below ground: the water leaving the unit reaches the soil through a distribution system, typically with elements bedded in gravel. Nothing of it shows at the surface, and the area remains usable — within certain limits. Sizing is the critical point

reszek.cim: It is not to be fitted to the space left over
reszek.szoveg: It is not to be fitted to the space left over Sizing the system properly is critical. With an undersized soakaway, backing up and the silting up of the soil can appear, leading to operating problems and costly remediation. This is not a theoretical risk but the most common after-the-fact fault in this type of system. The size required does not follow from the type of unit but from four figures: the daily volume, the soil's measured infiltration capacity, the groundwater situation, and the available area. The volume of wastewater arriving appears, in essence, as the volume the system has to dispose of. From this follows the most important practical rule: the soakaway cannot be sized to the space left in the yard. If the area required does not fit, the answer is not to make the soakaway smaller — another route for disposal has to be found. The conditions

reszek.cim: What has to be settled for infiltration
reszek.szoveg: What has to be settled for infiltration 01 Measured infiltration capacity. At the intended position and depth of the soakaway, by percolation test. It cannot be derived from a soil-type label. 02 The highest seasonal groundwater. Not today's water level. The relationship between the soakaway and the groundwater is a condition of operation. 03 The daily volume to be disposed of. It follows from the household's load; a greater load needs a proportionately larger area. 04 Enough free area. The area required, together with access for servicing and the later use of the ground. 05 Conveying the water by gravity or by pump. If the soakaway sits higher than the unit's outlet, a pump is needed. 06 Wells, water base protection, sensitivity classification. From a water protection standpoint, the point at which treated water enters the ground is an object in its own right. In the long run

reszek.cim: What ruins it, and what keeps it working
reszek.szoveg: What ruins it, and what keeps it working These cause trouble An undersized area — backing up, silting Seasonal groundwater rising to the level of the soakaway Compacting, paving or driving over the area Deep-rooted planting above the soakaway Neglected maintenance of the unit — the quality of the water leaving it deteriorates Directing rainwater into the system These keep it working Sizing based on measured data, with a margin A disposal level kept at an adequate distance from the groundwater Grass or shallow-rooted planting over the area Regular maintenance of the unit Draining rainwater separately Settling the area's future use in advance Next step

Sizing asks for measured data Whether infiltration is feasible stands or falls on how much water the soil actually absorbs. This has to be measured — the percolation test page shows how and when. Treated water disposal Percolation test Frequently asked questions

reszek.cim: What we are asked most often
reszek.szoveg: What we are asked most often How large a soakaway does a family of four need? We deliberately give no figure, because without the soil's measured infiltration capacity it would have no basis. The same household of four needs a far smaller area on one soil and several times as much on another. The occupancy is only one input — the measurement is the other. Does anything show at the surface? Typically not. The arrangement is below ground, with grass or shallow-rooted planting above it. What cannot go there: paving, compaction, vehicle traffic and deep-rooted trees. What happens if the soakaway is undersized? The water does not leave quickly enough, it backs up, the soil's pores silt up, and the system deteriorates step by step. Remediation usually means breaking out and rebuilding the soakaway — considerably more expensive than the measurement beforehand would have been. Can water be infiltrated in clay soil? With more difficulty, over a larger area, and in some places not at all. Measurement decides this, not the name of the soil. Where on-site disposal cannot be achieved, another route has to be examined — and it is worth turning to a specialist early.

Soil and infiltration capacity Calling the soil „sandy” or „clayey” is not enough on its own. The question is how fast the soil on site can take water — and that has to be measured, not named. The most important difference

reszek.cim: The name of the soil is not a sizing figure
reszek.szoveg: The name of the soil is not a sizing figure Calling the soil „sandy”, „clayey” or „cohesive” is not enough on its own to size an infiltration system. The substantive question is how at what rate and under what conditions the soil on site can accept water — that is infiltration capacity, and it has to be measured, not named. The soil of two neighbouring plots can both be called sandy while behaving quite differently because of their stratification, their compaction or an intervening clay layer. That is why Government Decree 147/2010 makes the characteristics of the soil one of the basic conditions for sizing a standalone system — not the name of the soil. Adequate infiltration capacity is not enough on its own either: the groundwater, the area available, the quantity of treated water and the environmental restrictions together determine the means of disposal. What can be found out

reszek.cim: Where can information about the soil come from?
reszek.szoveg: Where can information about the soil come from? The sources are not equivalent. The order below roughly follows their reliability — from the bottom up. 01 The experience of neighbours or of the area. A useful preliminary signal but not measured data: the layering can differ from plot to plot. Good for pre-screening, not for sizing. 02 Observing earlier excavation. Footings, a pool, a garden pit — these say a great deal about the layers and can be documented with photographs. They do not, however, measure the capacity to accept water. 03 An earlier geotechnical report. If one was prepared for the building's design, it is often available. Its date must be checked, and whether it covers the soakaway's intended position. 04 Percolation test. This measures directly what sizing needs: the soil's actual capacity to accept water, at the soakaway's intended position and depth. What the soil affects

Two separate effects The soil's type and layering affect… the difficulty and cost of the earthworks the stability of the excavation and whether shoring is needed the quality of the backfill around the tank on made ground, the bearing capacity and settlement whether a geotechnical report is needed The MEASURED infiltration capacity affects… whether the water can be disposed of on site at all the surface area and volume the soakaway requires whether that area fits within the free space available long-term reliability — silting up, backing up whether another route for water disposal has to be examined What has to be treated separately

Made ground and layered soil Made ground is a separate case: the material, age, compaction and thickness of the fill may be unknown, and the impression at the surface is misleading. On made ground neither bearing capacity nor infiltration can be estimated from the soil type — here testing is not optional. Layered soil likewise: beneath a freely draining upper layer there may be a sealing clay layer that holds the water. The soakaway then behaves quite differently at its intended depth than the surface promises. This is why the test has to be carried out at the soakaway's intended position and depth, not at some arbitrary point on the plot. The result

reszek.cim: Four possible outcomes — not „good” or „bad” soil
reszek.szoveg: Four possible outcomes — not „good” or „bad” soil 01 Indicative data is available. There is information, but it is an estimate or an old document. Enough for pre-screening, not for sizing. 02 Measurement is needed. The existing figure is insufficient or does not relate to where the soakaway will be. A percolation test follows. 03 Infiltration can be designed. On the measured value, on-site disposal is realistic; the area required can be calculated together with the daily volume of water. 04 An alternative means of disposal has to be examined. The soil will not take the volume required, or the area required will not fit. Another means of disposal then has to be examined. Next step

reszek.cim: Without the groundwater, the soil data is not enough either
reszek.szoveg: Without the groundwater, the soil data is not enough either Even soil that takes water well is not enough if the seasonal groundwater rises to the level of the soakaway, or if a water-protection restriction applies. The two figures have to be looked at together. Plot suitability overview Groundwater Frequently asked questions

reszek.cim: What we are asked most often
reszek.szoveg: What we are asked most often Is it enough that water drains well next door? It serves as a preliminary signal but is not enough for sizing. Layering can vary even within a plot, and the neighbour's soakaway may work at a different depth under a different load. The test has to be carried out on your own plot, at the intended position and depth. What exactly does a percolation test measure? How fast the soil absorbs water at the intended depth. Together with the daily volume to be disposed of, this value gives the infiltration area required. It cannot be derived from a soil-type label. I already have a geotechnical report for the building work. Is that enough? It is often a good starting point, but two things have to be checked: when it was prepared, and which point of the plot and what depth it covers. An investigation made for the foundations was not necessarily carried out at the soakaway's intended position and depth. Is on-site disposal impossible in clay soil? Not automatically, but it is harder and needs a larger area — and in some places it cannot be solved. Measurement decides this, not the name of the soil. Where on-site disposal cannot be achieved, another route has to be examined.

Special or industrial wastewater „Industrial wastewater” is not a single category, and it cannot be sized from headcount. Here the production technology and the laboratory data are the starting point. The underlying question

reszek.cim: Fifty people, or a fifty-person plant?
reszek.szoveg: Fifty people, or a fifty-person plant? The domestic wastewater of fifty people working in a plant and the process wastewater from the production of a fifty-person plant are not the same sizing task — not even when the headcount is the same. The composition of domestic wastewater is broadly predictable. The composition of process wastewater, by contrast, is set by the production process: the effluent of a winery, a dairy and an abattoir differ radically even from one another. So „industrial wastewater” is not a single uniform category, and it cannot be sized from headcount. Here the starting point is the technology and the laboratory data. What has to be known

The process data 01 Separating the two wastewater streams. How much is sanitary (domestic) and how much is of process origin. In many cases they can be treated separately — and that is the cheapest solution. 02 The production technology. What is made, by what processes, and from what raw and ancillary materials. 03 Working pattern. How many shifts, how many days a week, how many operating days a year. 04 Seasonality. A winery produces something entirely different at harvest than in winter. Seasonality is what sets the peak load. 05 Water flow. Average and maximum m³/day, and the hourly or per-shift peak. 06 Laboratory parameters. BOD5, COD, suspended solids, and depending on the industry fats/oils, nitrogen, phosphorus, pH, temperature. The exact list is always set by the technology. 07 Existing pre-treatment. Whether a grease trap, screen, settling tank or balancing tank is already in place. The two routes

What follows from the data Domestic-type stream The composition of the wastewater resembles household effluent The process stream can be separated off, or is negligible Conventional biological treatment can be applied Sizing starts from headcount and water consumption Laboratory analysis is typically not a precondition Process stream The load arising from production is decisive Sampling and laboratory analysis are required Pre-treatment and balancing have to be examined Industry-specific discharge limits apply Bespoke engineering design, not a catalogue size What we will not undertake from a template

reszek.cim: Why there is no capacity table here
reszek.szoveg: Why there is no capacity table here The current ÖkoTech content mentions the biological treatment of abattoir, dairy and winery wastewater as achievable. That professional capability may well exist, but no automatic sizing can be built on it on a website — because the inlet water quality and the pre-treatment required differ from project to project. So there is no capacity table and no model recommendation on this page. What there is: a list of the data required, and the route to a feasibility study. Without laboratory data the first step is sampling — not a quote. This is not timidity. A badly sized industrial system does not waste the investor's money first — it makes meeting the discharge requirements impossible, and that is considerably harder to correct after the fact. Next step

reszek.cim: Let us start with the technology
reszek.szoveg: Let us start with the technology Write and tell us what the activity is, over how many shifts, in what annual rhythm, and whether there are already laboratory results. From that we can say whether the existing data is enough for a feasibility study or whether sampling has to come first. When you need an expert Get in touch Frequently asked questions

reszek.cim: What we are asked most often
reszek.szoveg: What we are asked most often We have no laboratory results. Can we still request a quote? Not a quote, responsibly, but a feasibility discussion yes. From the technology, the working pattern and the flow we can say what analysis is needed and what order of magnitude is involved. For sizing, however, laboratory data is unavoidable. Can the sanitary and process wastewater be separated? In many plants yes, and it is often the cheapest solution: the domestic stream can be treated in the usual way while the process stream receives separate pre-treatment. It is worth examining this at the design stage. Which laboratory parameters are needed? The minimum is typically BOD5, COD and suspended solids; beyond that, depending on the industry, fats and oils, nitrogen, phosphorus, pH and temperature. The exact list is set by the technology — which is why we ask about the production process first. Is there anything you will not take on? Yes, and we say so in advance. There are process wastewaters that cannot be treated biologically, or only with substantial pre-treatment. Where that is the case we say so during the feasibility study — not after the quote.

Treated water disposal Choosing the unit gets you halfway. The volume leaving each day does not vanish: it has to be disposed of somewhere — and that is the harder question. Why this is a topic of its own

reszek.cim: Choosing the unit does not close the project
reszek.szoveg: Choosing the unit does not close the project Choosing the biological treatment unit gets you halfway. The other half is where the treated water leaving the unit goes, and by what means — and this has to be settled at the design stage, not in the week of installation. The volume leaving each day is roughly the volume of wastewater arriving. It does not vanish: it has to be disposed of somewhere. The route for disposal is therefore a precondition of quoting, not an afterthought — where it is unsettled, the project is not ready for a quote. This section goes through the routes for disposal and the conditions attaching to each. It offers no universal recommendation: the outcome is a likely route for disposal, together with the plot data each needs and any investigations that may be required. Routes for disposal

reszek.cim: Where can the treated water go?
reszek.szoveg: Where can the treated water go? Three main routes, with different technical and regulatory conditions. They are not equivalent alternatives: the first is the most common, the third a separate technical and legal branch. Soakaway infiltration The most common on-site solution: disposing of the already treated water below ground, in the soil. It turns on the soil's measured capacity to accept water, on the groundwater and on the free area. Soakaway infiltration→ Drainage field With a septic tank system the field formed in the soil is not an accessory but part of the treatment. Its space requirement is therefore larger, and it cannot be moved freely. Drainage field→ Reed bed disposal Use within the plot on a planted area. With an exact technical definition and clear limits on use — it is not the same as regulated agricultural irrigation. Reed bed disposal→ The most common misunderstanding

Soakaway infiltration or drainage field? After an active biological system — infiltration Treatment has taken place IN THE UNIT The soakaway serves to dispose of the outlet water The space requirement is typically smaller Sizing is a function of the daily volume and the measured infiltration The position can be chosen, with due care After a septic tank — a drainage field ANAEROBIC pre-treatment takes place in the tank A significant part of the aerobic process takes place IN THE FIELD The field is part of the technology, not a discharge The space requirement is therefore typically larger The legislation itself names a facility “with a drainage field” What it depends on

reszek.cim: What decides which route can be considered?
reszek.szoveg: What decides which route can be considered? These act together. A single unfavourable factor can rewrite the direction, but no single favourable one is enough on its own. 01 The soil's measured infiltration capacity. Not the soil's name. This determines whether the soil will accept the daily volume, and over what area. 02 The groundwater's seasonal maximum. Not today's water level. The relationship between the soakaway and the groundwater is a basic condition of operation. 03 The daily volume leaving the unit. It follows from the load, and it directly determines the soakaway's size. 04 The free area available. The area required also has to fit — after the house, the well, the driveway and the structures planned. 05 Wells and water base protection. From a water protection standpoint, the point at which treated water enters the ground is an object in its own right. 06 Area sensitivity classification. In a highly sensitive area, separate conditions apply to discharge into the geological medium. What this section does not do

reszek.cim: There is no universal recommendation for disposal
reszek.szoveg: There is no universal recommendation for disposal The route for disposal is plot-specific. The same unit may need a different solution on two neighbouring plots — and in some places on-site disposal cannot be achieved at all. What we give here is therefore not a recommendation but conditions and a decision path. Discharge to a surface watercourse is therefore a separate technical and legal branch: it requires a water-rights permit and compliance with discharge conditions, and cannot be treated as a simple alternative to on-site disposal. Where it arises, a qualified designer and consultation with the authority follow. Nor do we state a specific price. The cost level of the different arrangements differs — a larger soakaway, pumped conveyance, a special arrangement all bear on cost — but that can only be read in the context of the project as a whole, not on its own. Next step

reszek.cim: Start with the most common route
reszek.szoveg: Start with the most common route On most family home projects, infiltration is the first route to examine. Where the soil and the groundwater permit it, it is the simplest solution — and it becomes clear at once what has to be measured for it. When you need an expert Soakaway infiltration Frequently asked questions

reszek.cim: What we are asked most often
reszek.szoveg: What we are asked most often How much water leaves the unit each day? Roughly as much as the wastewater arriving — biological treatment breaks down the pollutant load, it does not make the water disappear. The soakaway therefore cannot be sized to the space left in the yard: it has to be sized to the daily volume. If the soil is good, is water disposal settled? Not necessarily. Even with soil that takes water well, high seasonal groundwater, a tight free area, a well nearby or the area's sensitivity classification can be obstacles. The soil is one condition, not the only one. Can the water be discharged into the stream or the ditch? This is a separate technical and legal question: it requires a water-rights permit and compliance with discharge requirements, and cannot be considered at every site. It is not a simple alternative to on-site infiltration — it has to be discussed with a qualified designer and with the authority. Can I water the garden with the treated water? Use within the plot carries technical and usage conditions, and not every use is permissible. We treat this on a separate page, because the question is a sensitive one: ornamental planting is one thing and food crops another, and regulated agricultural reuse is a separate legal category again. When is an expert needed? If the groundwater is unknown, the infiltration capacity has not been measured, the plot may fall within a designated water base protection zone, a surface receiving water comes into play, or the project is larger or non-domestic. Separate pages work through these.

Vehicle loading and access Two separate questions: can the machine get in for the installation, and does access remain for servicing. The second is what is most often left out — and what causes trouble years later. Two separate kinds of access

reszek.cim: Installation and operation need different things
reszek.szoveg: Installation and operation need different things One question is how the machinery needed for installation gets onto the plot, and how the tank is placed. This is one-off, but on installation day there is no alternative to it. The other is how the system stays reachable during use and servicing. That is a lasting requirement: the cover must remain openable and the unit inspectable and maintainable — years later too. The most important constraint

reszek.cim: No vehicle traffic over the tank
reszek.szoveg: No vehicle traffic over the tank Over a standard plastic tank, vehicle traffic cannot run directly, and a road or pavement cannot simply be built over it. This is a product-specific structural limit, not timidity. Where vehicle loading is unavoidable — because the only room is under the driveway, for instance — a separate, properly sized concrete chamber and prior technical consultation are required. This can be done, but it is a design decision and a cost item, not an afterthought. The same applies to the area above the soakaway: there, compaction and paving impair the operation rather than endanger the structure — but the consequence is a failure just the same. Access for installation

What to check before construction Most of these can be settled in advance from photographs, without a site visit. 01 Gate width and height. The narrowest point of the drive, the actual dimension between the gate posts. 02 The drive's load-bearing capacity. On soft ground, freshly made ground or beside an embankment, the machine may not get in. 03 Overhanging obstacles. Overhead power lines, branches, a canopy — height constrains just as width does. 04 The route for lifting the tank in. The tank does not roll: it has to be lifted into place. Where the machine will stand and the route for the lift have to be settled in advance. 05 Where the excavated soil goes. The soil out of the excavation takes up a considerable volume. With nowhere to put it, it has to be carted away — a cost and extra traffic. 06 Planting and paving to be retained. What must not be disturbed, and what can be reinstated afterwards. Access for servicing

reszek.cim: What is needed for the long term
reszek.szoveg: What is needed for the long term This is the part most often left out of the design — and it causes the most irritation years later. 01 The cover should open freely: no paving, flower bed, stored material or parked car over it 02 There should be room enough around the unit to work 03 The area over the soakaway should remain inspectable 04 The power supply and the controls should be accessible 05 Where emptying is needed, it should be reachable by a lorry 06 Planting should not encroach: a deep-rooted tree near the cover will cause trouble later Next step

reszek.cim: Now you know what you have to obtain
reszek.szoveg: Now you know what you have to obtain You have been through the seven topics. The next page shows, source by source, where each of the things you need can be obtained and how reliably — and what to do about what you do not know. Plot suitability overview How to gather the plot data Frequently asked questions

reszek.cim: What we are asked most often
reszek.szoveg: What we are asked most often Can the tank go under the driveway? Only with a separate, properly sized concrete chamber and prior technical consultation. Vehicle traffic cannot run directly over a standard plastic tank. If there is no other room, this has to be settled at the design stage, because it carries consequences for cost and construction. What happens if paving is later built over the cover? The cover has to remain openable and accessible, or inspection and maintenance become impossible. If you are planning paving, say so in advance — the siting will then be different from the start, or the paving will have an openable section. Can access be pre-screened from photographs? Most questions, yes. The narrowest point of the drive, the gate, overhanging cables, the intended position and its surroundings can be judged well from photographs. If uncertainty remains after that, an on-site survey is warranted.

Wells and protective distance It would be convenient to give a single protective distance. That would be misleading: the answer depends on the type of well, on the water base protection situation, and on where the water is actually disposed of. The first thing to settle

reszek.cim: The tank and the soakaway are two separate objects
reszek.szoveg: The tank and the soakaway are two separate objects From a water protection standpoint, the sealed treatment tank position and the point where the treated or pre-treated water actually enters the ground. The tank is a sealed structure; the soakaway, by contrast, is precisely the object where water enters the geological medium. The question about the well concerns the latter above all. This distinction appears in ÖkoTech's current guidance too, and it is a sound starting point. It does not follow, however, that the same holds for every type of well and every area classification. Why we give no single figure

reszek.cim: There is no universal answer to “how many metres?”
reszek.szoveg: There is no universal answer to “how many metres?” It would be convenient to give a single protective distance. That would be misleading, because the answer depends on several circumstances at once: the well's type (dug, bored, deep), legal status, the water base protection situation, the direction of flow of the subsurface water, the groundwater level, and the position of the actual point of disposal. For highly sensitive areas, Government Decree 147/2010 expressly ties the possibility of infiltrating treated wastewater to the water base protection rules, and Government Decree 123/1997 assigns protective zones and areas to water bases. These do not amount to a single figure in metres but to a site-dependent geometry. If someone gives a single general number, it either relates to one particular situation or is not precise enough. So here we show instead what data the answer is assembled from. What you need to provide

reszek.cim: What data is needed about the well?
reszek.szoveg: What data is needed about the well? The more of these are known, the fewer expert rounds are needed. Both your own wells and the neighbours' have to be accounted for. 01 The type of well. Dug, drilled or deep. A dug well typically draws on the groundwater, a deeper drilled well on a different aquifer — so the risk picture differs. 02 Its use. Drinking water, irrigation, watering livestock, or not in use. Use for drinking water is judged considerably more strictly. 03 Its exact position. Relative to the plot boundary and the intended soakaway, marked on a site plan. Including wells on neighbouring plots. 04 Its depth and strata, if known. For a bored well the well documentation may contain them. It shows which aquifer it reaches. 05 Documentation and legal status. Whether it has a permit or has been registered. This is not a question for the wastewater project, but it affects the expert assessment. 06 A designated water base protection area. Whether a protection zone or perimeter affects the plot. This has to be checked from an official source, not estimated. The result

Four possible outcomes 01 No obvious conflict. On the data known, the intended arrangement meets no visible obstacle. This is not an official certificate but the result of pre-screening. 02 Further well data is needed. The well's type, depth or documentation is missing. Without these the assessment rests on nothing. 03 A water base protection check is needed. The plot may fall within a designated protection zone, or the classification is uncertain. Whether infiltration is permitted has to be established from an official source. 04 The soakaway's position has to be changed. The layout can be rearranged so that the point of disposal sits further away, in a different direction, or in a more favourable position relative to the flow of subsurface water. Next step

reszek.cim: Moving the soakaway needs room for it
reszek.szoveg: Moving the soakaway needs room for it Moving it because of a well is only a solution if there is somewhere to move it to. The next page is about the area genuinely free — what remains once the house, the driveway and the utilities are accounted for. reszek.cim: What we are asked most often
reszek.szoveg: What we are asked most often Does a well rule the system out from the start? Not in itself. The sealed tank and the point where the treated water is disposed of are separate objects, and it is usually the latter that raises the real question. Judging it, however, requires knowing the well's type, its use, its position and the area's water base protection situation. Why do you not say how many metres are needed from the well? Because a single figure would not be true in every situation. Judging the distance depends on the well's type and depth, the direction of groundwater flow, the area's sensitivity classification, and whether a designated water base protection area is involved. A general number here would mislead more than it would help. Does a neighbour's well have to be taken into account? Yes. For water protection purposes it is not the plot boundary that governs but the actual relationship between the well and the point of disposal. Neighbouring wells are therefore worth marking on the site plan. There is an old, unused well on the plot. Does it matter? It can. A well no longer in use but not sealed may remain an open route towards the subsurface water. Its position and condition are worth reporting, because they affect the expert assessment.
When you need an expert Two mistakes cost the same: an unnecessary round with a specialist, and a test that was never done. This page draws the line between them. Two mistakes, at the same price

reszek.cim: The unnecessary round and the test never done
reszek.szoveg: The unnecessary round and the test never done On an ordinary family-home plot, several basic figures obtained remotely may be enough to set the first technical direction — and then a round with a specialist is wasted cost and time. There are situations, however, where an online pre-screening cannot substitute for an on-site or qualified expert investigation. A „we will sort it ourselves” attitude then costs more than the expert — because the mistake has to be put right on a system already built. This page draws the line between them: when your own data is enough, when an on-site survey is needed, and when a specialist we do not provide is required. The line

reszek.cim: When the data is enough, and when it is not
reszek.szoveg: When the data is enough, and when it is not Remote pre-screening is usually enough An ordinary family-home project, with domestic wastewater Known and documented soil and groundwater data There is no well nearby, or its position is settled Not a sensitive or highly sensitive area Ample free area The pipe exit level is known or can still be designed Here a specialist is needed An unknown or merely estimated seasonal groundwater level There is no measured infiltration data and on-site disposal is the aim A designated water base protection zone, or an uncertain well situation A highly sensitive area A very small or heavily built-up plot A plan to discharge to a surface watercourse A larger-capacity, institutional or non-domestic project To whom, and with what

Which specialist for which question? These are not the same competence. Going to the wrong specialist wastes as much time as having none. 01 ÖkoTech technical surveyor. Placement, levels, access, the system's arrangement, the plot brief. Settles what is a question of the unit and the installation. 02 Geotechnical engineer. Soil mechanics, layering, bearing capacity, percolation testing. Needed when the soil's behaviour is the question. 03 Hydrogeologist. Subsurface waters, flow conditions, water base protection assessment. Needed when the water's path is the question — not the soil's. 04 A qualified mechanical or hydraulic engineer. Permitting and construction drawings, surface watercourse discharge, sizing larger projects. They are the ones who speak to what is the designer's responsibility. 05 Accredited laboratory. Water quality analysis. Indispensable on a larger or non-domestic project, or where a discharge requirement applies. 06 The authority. Whether a permit can be obtained, the water-rights permit, area classification. No one else can speak to this with any validity. What an ÖkoTech survey does not settle

reszek.cim: The limits of our own remit
reszek.szoveg: The limits of our own remit Our on-site survey is a technical service: it records the levels, the layout, the access and the visible risks, and produces a structured plot brief. That closes a good deal of uncertainty. What it does not decides: whether a permit can be granted, the water base protection assessment, the flow conditions of the subsurface water, and the sizing that falls to a qualified designer's responsibility. In these the supplier of the unit has no competence — and anyone who promises otherwise is undertaking what they are not authorised to do. We say this deliberately: a project is safe when everyone speaks within their own remit. What to take to the specialist

reszek.cim: What makes it quicker and cheaper
reszek.szoveg: What makes it quicker and cheaper A specialist's time is expensive. The more of these are available, the less of it is needed. 01 A site plan with the house, the well, the driveway and the intended position of the system 02 Where the wastewater pipe leaves, and its invert depth 03 Whatever is known about the soil and groundwater — with documents and dates 04 An earlier geotechnical report, if there is one 05 The well's data sheet or documentation 06 The size of the household and the intended manner of use 07 Photographs of the intended installation position and of the driveway 08 The name of the settlement and the land registry number — to check the classification Next step

reszek.szoveg: Tell us where you have got to If it is not clear which route your project falls on, write and tell us what you know — the name of the municipality, the plot's characteristics and the size of the household. We will say whether a remote pre-screening is enough, or which investigation is warranted. Treated water disposal Get in touch Frequently asked questions

reszek.cim: What we are asked most often
reszek.szoveg: What we are asked most often Why is an on-site survey not always enough? Because a survey is a technical service, not a regulatory procedure and not a designer's declaration. It settles the levels, the layout and the access, but it cannot pronounce on water base protection or on whether a permit will be granted. Who pays for the specialist investigation? Geotechnical, hydrogeological and design work are services in their own right, with their own cost. That is precisely why it matters to decide in advance whether they are needed — on many projects they are not, and it would be money wasted. What changes on a larger project? Alongside capacity, the permitting and operating model become relevant too, and water quality, discharge limits and laboratory data enter the picture. Such a project needs design expertise and — for discharge to a watercourse — water-rights expertise.

Who operates the system after handover? With a per-property arrangement, the owner, with our service support behind them. With a central plant the operator may be the local authority or the regional utility — at Bakonypéterd, for instance, Pannon-Víz Zrt. took it over. Is there grant funding for a project like this? There has been and there may be — the Csikvánd project was delivered under the Rural Development Programme. It is worth following the current calls through the local authority and the grant portals; we can help put the technical content together.
