reszek.cim: What do the water quality parameters mean?
reszek.szoveg: What do the water quality parameters mean? At the end of the process treated water leaves the unit. The wording matters here: this is not „clean water” in any general sense, and certainly not drinking water How clean it is, is decided not by the eye but by measured parameters. COD — chemical oxygen demand Put simply, it shows numerically how much oxygen-demanding pollutant load remains in the water. The lower it is, the less degradable pollution is left. BOD₅ — biochemical oxygen demand It measures the same load, but the biologically degradable narrowed to the part, over five days. Together the two show what the biology accomplished and what was left after it. Suspended solids It shows mennyi solid, suspended matter remained in the water — that is, how well the activated sludge and the water separated during settlement. Nitrogen and phosphorus Nutrients that burden the receiving water. Testing may cover these too; which of them matters on a given project is decided by how the treated water is disposed of. This says far more than that the outlet water looks clear looks clear. The specific discharge values are worth reading with their measurement conditions — they are in the unit's technical data sheet: A.B.Clear technical data.

Division of responsibility The owner's responsibility A regular visual check — is the aeration working The settlement test on the activated sludge Checking and handling the sludge bag Keeping the operating log Observing what may and may not go into the system Notifying the service team of a fault indication The service team's responsibility Periodic servicing and inspection Maintaining and replacing the compressor and membrane Checking and setting the controller Repairing faults the owner cannot resolve Commissioning, and restarting after a long shutdown Parts replacement What the owner checks

A regular feladatok We deliberately do not put numbers on the frequencies here — see below for why. The unit's current operating manual records the exact schedule. 01 Aeration. Whether the compressor is running and there is bubbling in the aerated chamber. This is the single most important sign: with no aeration the biology stops. 02 Condition of the activated sludge. A settlement test with a measuring cylinder: how long the sludge takes to settle and in what proportion. This shows the health of the system. 03 Sludge bag. Condition, fullness, handling. This is the owner's part of the A.B.Clear sludge model. 04 General condition. Odour, the seal of the cover, the water surface, an unusual noise from the compressor. 05 Operating log. What you checked and when, and what you observed. Not bureaucracy: in the event of a fault it shows how long the symptom has been present. Substances

Power failure, absence, fault indication Power failure. The system rides out a short outage. With a sustained loss of power the absence of aeration degrades the biology — after a longer outage it is worth watching how the system behaves. Absence. For a shorter absence the system stays in operation. A gap of several months calls for a separate procedure. The unit's current documentation records the exact thresholds. Fault indication. If the controller indicates a fault, or an unusual smell, noise or change in the water surface is noticed, that warrants a service call. These are not repairs for the owner. Next step

reszek.szoveg: And what does all this cost? Operation carries a cost too: energy, parts, servicing, consumables. The cost factors page works through them — without a specific price, but item by item. Sludge bag technology Cost factors Frequently asked questions

reszek.cim: What we are asked most often
reszek.szoveg: What we are asked most often How much time does it take each month? The regular visual check takes a few minutes, and the settlement test is short too. We publish no specific annual time figure at present, because it is not consistently documented — but the order of magnitude falls in the regular rather than the time-consuming category. What counts is the regularity. What happens if I skip the checks? Nothing breaks straight away — and that is exactly the danger. The condition of the biology degrades gradually, the outlet water quality falls, and by the time there is a visible sign, recovery is already a longer process. That is why the operating log matters. Is a maintenance contract required? Regular professional servicing is strongly recommended, and the guarantee terms may be tied to it. We agree the exact terms at the point of purchase, because they depend on the product and the contract. Does it really need no emptying? Under normal operation the sludge bag solution does away with regular emptying — but that does not mean there is nothing to do about the sludge. Handling the bag is the owner's task, and in an exceptional situation other intervention may be needed. The sludge bag page sets this out in detail.

Plot and load conditions The technology suits how you use the property — but can the actual project be built? Where the tank goes and where the water goes are two separate questions. Two questions, one page

reszek.cim: From technological suitability to project suitability
reszek.szoveg: From technological suitability to project suitability The previous pages were about whether the technology suits the way you use the property. This page is about whether your actual project can be built: whether the load is right, and whether the system can be installed on that particular plot. The two cannot be separated, because they bear on each other: a greater load needs a larger unit and a larger infiltration area, and a narrow plot is exactly what limits that. The load side

reszek.cim: What has to be known about the use?
reszek.szoveg: What has to be known about the use? 01 Permanent occupancy. How many people live at or regularly stay in the property. 02 Actual water use. At an existing property, from the water bill — that is more accurate than headcount. 03 Peak load. How large, how long and how often. A regular weekend surplus is not the same as a celebration twice a year. 04 Absence. The longest period expected during which the system receives no load. 05 Planned expansion. If the occupancy will grow within two or three years, that has to be allowed for now. The installation side

reszek.cim: What has to be known about the plot?
reszek.szoveg: What has to be known about the plot? Where the tank goes and where the treated water goes are TWO separate questions — they cannot be handled with a single „will it fit?” 01 Soil and measured infiltration capacity. This determines whether the treated water can be disposed of on site, and over how large an area. 02 Groundwater. The seasonal maximum. It bears on anchoring the tank, and separately on infiltration. 03 Free area. What remains once the house, the well, the driveway and the utilities are accounted for — including access for servicing. 04 The depth at which the wastewater pipe leaves the building. This determines what level the unit's inlet can sit at, and whether a riser or a pumping station is needed. 05 Electrical preparation. The unit needs a properly protected electrical connection built for it. 06 Vehicle loading and access. Vehicles cannot be driven over the tank without a separate arrangement, and the system has to remain accessible later on. What changes the design, and what stops it

reszek.cim: What we are asked most often
reszek.szoveg: What we are asked most often How deep does the wastewater pipe have to be? We give no figure for this at present, because our public material carries two different values for the permitted riser height, and there is no published data for the larger models. Until that is reconciled, we say so in discussion on the specific project — so that anyone relying on the website is not misled. What if the pipe is too deep? A riser element or a pumping chamber then comes into play. Both are solutions, but with cost and operating consequences: a pumping station means capital cost, electricity consumption and one more mechanical component to maintain. Does it need a separate electrical installation? Yes, the unit needs a properly protected electrical connection. Building it is typically part of the works — worth settling early who carries it out.

Biological wastewater treatment Micro-organisms break down the organic pollutants in the wastewater — the same process that runs at large plants, at the scale of a single property. But it does not suit every property without a sewer. What it means

A living process, not filtration The essence of active biological treatment is that the organic pollutants in household wastewater are broken down by micro-organisms — the same process that runs at large treatment plants, only at the scale of a single property. The bacteria need oxygen for this, which aeration supplies to the system. This is fundamentally different from a sealed holding tank, which only collects, and from a septic tank, where a substantial part of the treatment continues in the ground. Here the great majority of the treatment happens inside the unit itself. One key element of the process is the activated sludge. This is not „dirt” to be got rid of as soon as possible but a medium rich in micro-organisms that takes an active part in the treatment — which is why it requires controlled conditions. So aerated and unaerated stages alternate in the system: in the former the air supply provides oxygen for the aerobic processes, in the latter the more oxygen-poor environment assists other biological processes. The domestic wastewater enters the system. Physical and biological processes take place in the various chambers. The micro-organisms break down a substantial part of the organic pollutants. The activated sludge and the water separate. Treated water leaves the system, and surplus sludge is produced along the way. The system has two outputs: the treated water, which has to be disposed of, and the surplus sludge, which has to be handled. The second is the one least talked about — yet long-term operation turns on it too. Almost every operating rule follows from this: a living biological process cannot be used in the same way as a sealed tank.
„Treated water” does not mean the water can be soaked away anywhere or used for anything — that has to be settled separately. What this page does not claim

reszek.cim: It does not suit every property without a sewer
reszek.szoveg: It does not suit every property without a sewer A biological system is a good choice in many situations, but it is not automatically right for every property without a mains sewer. The regularity of use, the load, the plot, the groundwater and whether the treated water can be disposed of all count — as does whether the owner will take on the prescribed checks. That last is the condition most often left unsaid. The unit is automatic but not unattended: it requires regular checks, maintenance and a sludge settlement test. If that cannot be taken on, the technology will not work well — regardless of whether it physically fits on the plot. So on this page we show not only who it suits but also who it does not. reszek.cim: What makes the biological system different
reszek.szoveg: What makes the biological system different Active biological system The great majority of the treatment happens IN THE UNIT It needs aeration, and so electricity It requires continuous or regular use The quality of the outlet water can be measured and documented Regular checks and sludge handling go with it The treated water then has to be disposed of Sealed holding tank and septic tank Sealed holding tank: it only collects, it does not treat — regular emptying Septic tank: anaerobic pre-treatment, the treatment continues IN THE GROUND A septic tank needs no electricity A septic tank needs more area because of the drainage field It tolerates long gaps better — relevant for a seasonal property The quality of the outlet water is harder to document Evidence

reszek.cim: What do the technical tests prove?
reszek.szoveg: What do the technical tests prove? With a treatment unit, „it cleans well” is not enough on its own. The important question is what what testing and what measured results supports the claim. The A.B.Clear technical documentation records EN 12566-3 conformity, along with accredited tests and VITUKI measurements. The figures published include COD, BOD₅, suspended solids, nitrogen and phosphorus values. These numbers show different sides of treatment performance — but without context they mislead. What matters is which unit, under what load and under what test conditions was measured. So we list no values on this page: we publish them with their measurement conditions where the documentation is available too. The standard, the declaration of performance and the laboratory results are not advertising claims. They are useful precisely because they show what was verified actually about the unit. Documents and certificates Frankly

reszek.cim: The advantage of A.B.Clear is not that it „suits everyone”
reszek.szoveg: The advantage of A.B.Clear is not that it „suits everyone” With a biological treatment unit, the strongest argument is not that it is modern, environmentally friendly or little trouble. Such claims do not help you decide. How the system works is better understood from how the technology is built: aerated and unaerated chambers, an activated sludge biological process, fine-bubble aeration and a membrane air blower. But even that is only a real advantage if the load and use of your property meet the conditions of the technology. So the most important question is not „how good is the A.B.Clear?” but whether this technology is right in your situation. Sometimes the right technical choice is the A.B.Clear. Sometimes it is another system. In the long run settling that in advance is worth more than adapting a badly chosen technology to real use later. What the system will not take

Mit not szabad beleengedni? Activated sludge is a living mass of bacteria. Whatever kills or paralyses it stops the treatment — and recovery can take weeks. 01 Bactericides and strong chemicals. Disinfectants, chlorine-based products, acidic drain cleaners in larger quantities. 02 Pharmaceutical residues in larger quantities. Antibiotics especially — killing bacteria is what they are for. 03 Fats and oils in large quantities. Cooking oil down the drain: it forms a film on the surface and impairs the oxygen transfer. 04 Non-degradable solids. Wet wipes, sanitary products, cat litter — these do not break down, they accumulate. 05 Paint, solvent, fuel. These are not household wastewater, and they damage the biology lastingly. 06 Rainwater. Not toxic, but it dilutes the wastewater and overloads the system hydraulically. Next step

reszek.cim: First, let us understand what happens
reszek.szoveg: First, let us understand what happens Once you understand how it works, every further question — maintenance, chemical sensitivity, under- and overloading — becomes self-evident. A few minutes, and the decision is easier afterwards. The A.B.Clear range How it works Frequently asked questions

reszek.cim: What we are asked most often
reszek.szoveg: What we are asked most often How much better is this than a septic tank? Not „better” but different. An active biological system gives a measurably better outlet water quality in a smaller space, in exchange for electricity and regular checks, and it likes continuous use. The septic tank is more forgiving on those counts but asks for more area. The choice turns on the usage profile. Does it smell? In normal operation, no. Odour typically signals a malfunction: inadequate aeration, overloading or damage to the biology. That is precisely why regular checks matter — odour is not something to put up with but a symptom. How much electricity does it use? We publish no specific consumption figure here, because it differs by model and is not consistently documented in our public material. Aeration requires continuous operation, so this energy consumption is a standing item — the cost factors page deals with it. What happens during a power failure? The system rides out a short outage: the bacterial community does not die immediately. With a sustained loss of power, the absence of aeration degrades the biology. If the power supply at the property is unreliable, that has to be flagged before the technology is chosen. Is a permit required? That depends on the project and the location, and the procedural rules change from time to time. So we give no general answer here — the project preparation section deals with it, always citing a current source. Applicability cannot be judged from national rules alone: the technical and local requirements applying to the particular property have to be checked too. Can a biological system be installed in high groundwater? This cannot be answered with a general yes.

reszek.cim: What we are asked most often (part 2)
reszek.szoveg: Two separate questions are involved: siting the tank and the onward handling of the treated water. Both are decided by the particular conditions of the plot, so they have to be examined separately. High groundwater situations What happens with clayey, poorly draining soil? The problem lies primarily in disposing of the treated water arises, not in the treatment itself. On such a plot one must not think automatically in terms of infiltration — the method of water disposal has to be settled before the size of the unit. Is a soil investigation or an on-site survey needed? That depends on the method of disposal used and on the plot's characteristics. Where the treated water enters the ground, measured soil and groundwater data cannot be avoided; where another method of disposal is in play, the investigation required differs. Percolation test Do parts have to be replaced? The system contains working mechanical components — an air blower, for instance — so maintenance or replacement will be needed over time. That is inherent to the technology, not a fault. An expected life is only worth publishing with verified figures tied to a model and a part, so we name no number here.
When it is not suitable A badly chosen system is not cheaper — it just takes longer for the cost to show. An honest „this is not for you” is worth more than any discount. Why this page exists

„No” is an answer too A badly chosen system is not cheaper — it just takes longer for the cost to show. So here we gather the situations where an active biological system is not a good starting point, or is one only on separate conditions. We keep two categories apart: what is a general limit of the technology itself, and what belongs to the A.B.Clear limits of a particular product. The two are not the same, and neither are their consequences. Two degrees of severity

Not every exclusion is final Absolute — a different technology is needed A lasting power supply cannot be assured A long, complete gap of several months without a proper procedure Non-domestic wastewater without prior investigation The system regularly receives a heavy chemical load at the property The owner will not take on the regular checks Conditional — investigation or a separate arrangement Disposal of the treated water not solved — the plot decides, not the technology High groundwater — a structural solution may handle it A commercial kitchen or a significant grease load — pre-treatment is needed A widely fluctuating load — a matter of operating mode and sizing A small plot or one hard to reach — a question of layout The most common causes

What makes a project fail? In our experience these cause most of the disappointment after the fact — and every one of them could have been found out in advance. 01 It does not megoldott water disposal. This does not rule out the technology; it stops the project. The tank fits — but the daily volume of outlet water has nowhere to go. 02 Capacity wrongly determined. The system does not become right merely by fitting physically. Under sustained overload the outlet water quality degrades; under sustained underload the biology weakens. 03 Chemical load. Where strong disinfectants or chlorine-based products are used regularly — in certain industrial or healthcare settings, for instance — the biology cannot work stably. 04 Operation not taken on. If the regular checks and sludge handling do not happen, the system degrades gradually. This is not an immediate failure, which is why it is often noticed late. 05 Absence or unreliability of the power supply. Aeration requires continuous operation. With a sustained loss of power the biology breaks down. 06 Legal or territorial restriction. The question is not the unit but whether disposing of the treated water is permitted in that place. That is a matter for the authority.

reszek.cim: What to look at instead, and when
reszek.szoveg: What to look at instead, and when If the problem is the long gap or the missing power supply, the septic tank system comes into play: it is passive, needs no electricity, and takes intermittent use better. In exchange it asks for more area, because a substantial part of the treatment happens in the ground. If the problem is the water disposal, changing technology does not help on its own — a septic tank needs a still larger area. Examining a sealed holding tank or another means of disposal then follows. If the wastewater not domestic in character, what follows is not a product choice but an engineering task: sampling, laboratory analysis and a feasibility study. Next step

reszek.cim: If this is not the direction
reszek.szoveg: If this is not the direction The comparison of solution types page sets the three options side by side against the same criteria. If you are unsure, that is where to continue. Exclusions and limiting conditions Comparing solution types Frequently asked questions

reszek.cim: What we are asked most often
reszek.szoveg: What we are asked most often Is it really not right for a holiday home? It is not that simple. A property used regularly — every weekend, for instance — is manageable. One used only in summer and left for several months in winter calls for a separate shutdown procedure, and there the passive system is worth examining too. Can I use cleaning products at all? Yes, in normal household quantities. What to avoid: large amounts of chlorine-based and strongly disinfectant products, acidic drain cleaner, and pouring cooking oil down the drain. This is no stricter than what most households can manage anyway. If it is not right now, could it be later? Yes, several conditional cases can be resolved. Water disposal can be built, a power supply can be run, a commercial kitchen load can be handled with pre-treatment. That is why we separate conditional from absolute exclusion — the two are not the same.
Who does it suit? Suitability follows not from whether it is a family home or a guesthouse but from how the property is used. Not a building type

The pattern of use decides The suitability of a biological system follows not from whether it is a family home, a farmstead or a guesthouse but from how how it is used the property is used. The same building type can be an ideal choice and a poor one. The baseline: a property in continuous or regular use, with wastewater that is predominantly domestic in character, where electricity is available, the treated water can be disposed of, and the owner will take on the prescribed checks. That is four conditions, and all four have to be met. The four conditions

When does it work well? 01 Regular use. The bacterial community needs a continuous supply of nutrient. Permanent occupation is ideal; regular weekend use is manageable; a gap of several months calls for a separate procedure. 02 Domestic-type wastewater. Kitchen, bathroom, WC, laundry. If process, industrial or commercial kitchen wastewater arrives as well, that calls for separate examination — not an automatic exclusion, but not automatically fine either. 03 Electricity. Aeration requires continuous operation. If a lasting power supply cannot be assured at the property, an active system is not a good starting point. 04 Water disposal that can be solved. The daily volume of outlet water has to have somewhere to go. That is a question of the plot and the ground conditions — and it is often the bottleneck, not the unit. Typical situations

reszek.szoveg: Where it works well, and where it needs a separate look Typically a good choice A permanently occupied family home with no mains sewer A farmstead with electricity where water disposal can be solved Replacing an existing cesspit at a permanently occupied property A guesthouse or smaller accommodation business open all year The sanitary block of an office or plant — with domestic wastewater A weekend house used regularly, every weekend This needs separate examination A holiday home used only in summer, with a long winter gap A restaurant or commercial kitchen — the kitchen load is a separate question An unreliable or intermittent power supply Disposal of the treated water not solved A widely fluctuating, unpredictable load Non-domestic wastewater of process origin

reszek.cim: Seasonal use is not a yes or no question
reszek.szoveg: Seasonal use is not a yes or no question A holiday home is a good example of why deciding by building type is not worth doing: the use of two „holiday homes” can differ more than that of two entirely different kinds of property. One is used almost every week all year, the second is occupied only in summer, the third is visited a few times a year. Biologically these are three different situations. A shorter absence — an otherwise regularly used property standing empty for a while. Regular but not continuous use — a recurring rhythm, at weekends for instance. A long, seasonal gap — for several months little or no wastewater arrives. That is the situation calling for a separate procedure. A shorter or regular absence is manageable — the controller may support a low-load mode, and the bacterial community survives. A complete gap of several months, however, calls for a separate operating or shutdown procedure. That is a planned process, not „switch it off and come back next year”. If use is strongly intermittent, the question is no longer capacity but the choice of technology: the passive septic tank system may then be the more relevant. We work through this in detail on the seasonal use page. Next step

An honest „this is not for you” saves more money than any discount on a badly chosen system. Plot and load conditions When it is not suitable Frequently asked questions

reszek.cim: What we are asked most often
reszek.szoveg: What we are asked most often Is it right for a weekend house? For regular weekend use yes, provided there is a permanent power supply and the controller supports low-load operation. If use is more intermittent than that — with long breaks of several months — the passive system is worth examining too. Is it suitable for a guesthouse? For an accommodation business open all year, typically yes. The sizing starts not from the bed count but from the occupancy, and if there is a restaurant of your own the kitchen load is a separate question — it may require pre-treatment. What if we are rarely at home? An occasional absence of a few days is no problem. A regular, longer absence is already a question of operating mode, and one of several months calls for a separate shutdown procedure. Tell us the longest absence you expect — that shows what has to be done. Can two households share one? Technically it can be done, but the load, the arrangement of the connection and who is responsible for operation have to be settled. Shared use typically stalls not on technical grounds but on the question of responsibility.

Installation requirements The success of the project is decided not by the tank's pit but by whether the drainage field is also put in place at the right size. Installing the whole system

reszek.cim: Not only the size of the pit
reszek.szoveg: Not only the size of the pit The success of the project is decided not by the tank's pit but by whether the drainage field is also put in place at the right size. So this page covers the installation requirements of the whole system. Under the regulations a septic tank system with a drainage field has to be sized taking account of the soil conditions, the depth of the subsurface water and the quantity of wastewater. In an area of high groundwater or high sensitivity, further conditions may apply. Installing the tank

What the manufacturer's requirements determine 01 Earthworks and the size of the pit. Matched to the size of the tank and the ground conditions. 02 Bedding. The material and thickness of the layer beneath the tank — the basis of its structural stability. 03 Backfill. Its material and the method of compaction as the manufacturer prescribes. 04 Cover and depth of earth. How much earth may go over the tank, and what use is permitted above it. 05 Inlet and outlet pipe levels. These determine whether a riser is needed. 06 Anchoring against groundwater. The anti-flotation solution where groundwater is high. 07 Ventilation. Necessary for the system to work properly. Installing the drainage field

What the plot determines These have to be determined independently of the tank, from the plot's own conditions. 01 The measured infiltration capacity of the soil — from a percolation test 02 The seasonally highest groundwater level 03 The genuinely free area available 04 The ground slope and whether gravity drainage is possible 05 The position of the well or wells, including those on neighbouring plots 06 The intended later use of the area over the field 07 The type of distribution element used and its associated layer build-up Who carries it out

Division of responsibility This may be the client or their own contractor Earthworks, excavating the pit Bedding and backfill as the manufacturer prescribes Laying the pipework from the house Constructing the drainage field Delivery Available as an ÖkoTech service Delivery to site Sizing the system — tank and field together Installation and commissioning Handover and training the owner These are separate service items

Exclusions and limiting conditions Not every solution can be installed on every property. Some things the law rules out, some merely call for a different technical arrangement, and some only call for more data. The three do not have the same consequence. Why it has its own page

reszek.cim: „No” is an answer too — and better in good time
reszek.szoveg: „No” is an answer too — and better in good time This page exists so that a poor decision and a pointless request for a quote can be avoided. We keep three things sharply apart: what is a legal gate, mi a product-specific limit, and what merely calls for a different technical arrangement. That distinction is the point. A legal exclusion cannot be solved by configuration; a deep inlet pipe can — with a pumping station. Result categories

reszek.cim: There are five kinds of answer — and only one of them means „no”
reszek.szoveg: There are five kinds of answer — and only one of them means „no” Ruled out Some conditions rule the solution out legally or technically. There is then no configuration that would solve it. Only on separate conditions The solution is feasible but calls for a different technical arrangement — a pumping station, a concrete surround or a larger drainage field, for instance. Further data needed It cannot be settled from the information available. Typically groundwater, soil or water disposal data is missing. Expert examination required The situation goes beyond the standard cases: non-domestic wastewater, a larger capacity or a complex plot. Another solution has to be examined That direction is unsuitable, but another exists. We say so even when the other is not our system. Legal and technical

reszek.cim: What rules it out, and what merely changes it
reszek.szoveg: What rules it out, and what merely changes it A legal or territorial gate — no configuration gets past it the mains sewer is technically available on the public land bordering the property, and the treatment plant capacity is there too; a water base protection or highly sensitive area, where separate conditions or a municipal programme apply to the installation; the project's capacity category calls for a different procedure; non-domestic wastewater — the standard route breaks off here, and examination decides. A technical or usage constraint — configuration may handle it an incoming pipe that is too deep — a pumping station can solve it; high groundwater — a different installation method comes into play; too little area for the drainage field — it points towards a different technology; there is no continuous power — it rules out the active direction, not the passive one; long stretches carrying no load — they change the choice of technology, not the feasibility; the owner will not take on the prescribed inspection and maintenance. Legal background

On the legal framework The legal framework for standalone wastewater treatment is set by the relevant government decree: it lays down the system categories, the installation requirements, and the inspection, maintenance and record-keeping duties that fall on the owner. The specific references and the text currently in force always have to be checked before publication, because both the regulations and administrative practice can change. The conditions that apply in your municipality are worth establishing with the competent authority. Next step

reszek.cim: Let us look at it for your situation
reszek.szoveg: Let us look at it for your situation From a few questions, the pre-screener shows which directions are in play, what drops out, and what data the decision still lacks. The result is indicative: it establishes neither plot suitability nor whether a permit can be obtained. Or request an on-site survey Solution type pre-screener

Solutions At a property with no sewer three kinds of system come into play, but they do not do the same thing: the sealed holding tank collects, the septic tank settles and partly treats, the biological unit genuinely cleans. Which of them is in play on a given plot is decided together by the use, the power supply, the soil and the disposal of the treated water. Three routes

What the three solutions do The choice is not a question of product category: the same plot calls for different solutions depending on how it is used. 01 The sealed holding tank collects. It does not treat the wastewater but stores it until the next emptying. It needs no electricity but does need regular emptying — for which the tanker has to reach the tank. No treated water is produced. Its place is where local conditions allow nothing at all to enter the ground. 02 The septic tank settles and partially treats. It works by gravity, without electricity. Pre-treatment takes place in the tank, while the actual cleaning happens largely in the soakaway field, in the ground — so it calls for soil that can take infiltration. It needs regular emptying and periodic dosing. 03 The biological unit genuinely cleans. The bacterial culture living in the tank breaks down the organic matter, and at the end of the process treated water that can be soaked away leaves the unit. This, however, requires a power supply and a regular load. Excluding conditions

What rules the solutions out It is a good choice if… there is power, use is permanent and the treated water can be disposed of → biological treatment unit; there is no electricity or use is intermittent, but the soil can take infiltration → septic tank; the load is above 50 people → a sized system, not a domestic unit. This is not the solution if… there is no electricity and there will not be — the biological system drops out, because the aeration is what sustains the treatment; cohesive, poorly draining soil — the septic tank drops out, because the treatment would largely take place in the ground; the local requirements allow nothing at all to enter the ground (a water base protection zone, for instance) — only the sealed holding tank then remains, which we do not manufacture. Frequently asked questions

reszek.cim: What we are asked most often
reszek.szoveg: What we are asked most often Which is the cheapest solution? The capital price and the annual running cost are two separate questions. The sealed holding tank is cheaper to install, but regular emptying grows year on year with the size of the household and the service tariffs. With a biological system the installation costs more, while the annual items are essentially independent of the size of the household. Is a permit needed for any of them? Yes, but not the same one. At household scale the municipal procedure is typically the one that applies; for a larger discharge a water permit is required. The exact procedure depends on the capacity, the method of discharge and the local regulations. What happens to the existing cesspit? On a replacement the method of decommissioning has to be settled (emptying, possibly backfilling), and whether its position affects the installation of the new system. This is part of the works, not an afterthought.

Larger and community systems Not a bigger version of a domestic unit. In terms of load, technology, operation and permitting it is a project category in its own right — with a different design route. The basic proposition

Not a bigger domestic unit A larger treatment project is not a bigger version of a domestic unit. In terms of load, technology, operation and permitting it is a project category in its own right, with a different design route and a different system of responsibility. The commonest mistake is for the project to start with residential logic: they ask how many people, pick a size, and monitoring, pre-treatment and operation only come up at the end. On a larger system these are not details — they determine the structure of the project. So this section does not recommend a product but categorise: whether this is a standardisable domestic load, a modular community system, or a wholly bespoke engineered one. Three concepts

What must not be combined PE — population equivalent The unit of biodegradable ORGANIC load 1 PE = 60 g BOD5 per day This also determines the legal category (1–50 PE) Measurable by laboratory analysis It is NOT the same as the daily volume of water m³/day and „persons” m³/day = HYDRAULIC load, the volume of water arriving Read from the water meter; a measured figure at an existing facility „Persons” = an approximation of use, not a sizing unit At an institution or a plant, „persons” is particularly misleading The three figures have to be stated separately A correction

reszek.cim: The claim “1 PE = 135 litres per person per day” is wrong
reszek.szoveg: The claim “1 PE = 135 litres per person per day” is wrong Our earlier material said in one place that 1 population equivalent means a water consumption of 135 litres per person per day. We correct that: the population equivalent is a unit of organic load, not volume of water. The figure of 135 litres per person per day can at most remain our own hydraulic design baseline — if the engineering team still works with it and can document it. But the two concepts have to be kept terminologically apart. On a larger project this is not hair-splitting: the water consumption and organic load of an institution with a commercial kitchen stand in quite a different relation to one another than a dwelling's do. Four forms of system

reszek.cim: What kind of arrangement is in play?
reszek.szoveg: What kind of arrangement is in play? We do not work with product names but with system architecture: what kind of arrangement suits the facility. The specific unit follows from that, not the other way round. 01 Modular — several standard units linked together. Capacity built up in stages, units that can be taken off line. Our own example is the Bakonypéterd project: a central plant made up of four 50-person units. 02 A purpose-built high-capacity tank plant. A circular-section system manufactured for larger capacity, with a single unified process and control architecture. 03 Containerised arrangement. Where the installation circumstances or the need to relocate warrant it. 04 Bespoke engineered technology. For special, non-domestic wastewater. Here the main question is no longer the form of the tank but what pre-treatment or process modification is needed ahead of the biological stage. The pages in this section

reszek.szoveg: Where are you in the project? The order follows the logic of the project: category, load, technology, then operation and permitting. reszek.cim: What we are asked most often
reszek.szoveg: What we are asked most often What changes above 50 people? The category of standalone treatment under Government Decree 147/2010 extends to a load of 1–50 PE. Above that the project follows a different regulatory and permitting route, sizing becomes the task of a qualified designer, and monitoring and operating responsibility appear at a different level too. Several smaller units or one large one? Both are real routes, and the choice depends on the project. A modular arrangement allows capacity to be built up in stages and units to be taken off line; a purpose-built large plant can be designed as a more unified process and control system. The overview page works through this. Can abattoir or dairy wastewater be treated? Special loads can be handled on the basis of bespoke engineering analysis. This is not automatic suitability: sampling, laboratory data and a feasibility study come first. A standard plant is not automatically suitable for any industrial wastewater. Who will operate it? This has to be settled before the quote, not at handover. A larger system needs a named responsible operator, regular checks, an operating log and typically sampling too.
Capacity and project categories Three different things tend to get run together: the legal category, the boundary of the product range, and the project's actual load. Three separate categories

reszek.cim: What our site has until now run together
reszek.szoveg: What our site has until now run together Three different things tend to be spoken of as capacity, and they are not the same: the legal category, the boundary of ÖkoTech's product ranges, and the project's actual load. The statutory boundary is clear: standalone treatment under Government Decree 147/2010 extends to at most 50 population equivalent. That is a genuine regulatory dividing line — above it a different design and permitting route follows. The product boundary and the actual load, however, do not coincide with it, and at present our own communication is not consistent about this either. We say so here rather than papering over it. The categories

reszek.cim: Four bands, four different project routes
reszek.szoveg: Four bands, four different project routes The exact figures for the boundaries will appear here after internal validation. The structure of the categories, however, is already usable. 01 Standard standalone range. A domestic-type load, a catalogue model, the usual arrangement. This is the legal category too, up to 50 PE. 02 Modular transitional range. Several standard units linked together. The load exceeds the standalone category, but the technology is still built from known elements. 03 Large-plant product range. A tank or containerised system built specifically for large capacity, with unified control. 04 Bespoke industrial route. Non-domestic wastewater. Here capacity does not categorise on its own — the technology and the laboratory data decide. What changes when the boundary is crossed

Not only the size Below 50 PE The standalone treatment category under Decree 147/2010 A catalogue model can be chosen A simpler design route The owner may be the operator The inspection and documentation duties are simpler Above 50 PE It leaves the standalone category A qualified designer sizes it A different permitting route, different documentation A named responsible operator is required Operating log, self-monitoring, and typically sampling too The discharge requirements have to be examined separately „Persons” as a figure for communication

How far it takes you „How many people?” is user-friendly, and for a domestic-type, known pattern of use it is a good approximation. Most of the market starts there for a reason. At a guesthouse, an institution or a plant, however, the bed count and the staff headcount particularly misleading: the same number of „persons” can mean an entirely different volume of water and organic load. There, categorisation has to rest on PE, m³/day, peak load and, where needed, laboratory data. So we use „persons” as an entry figure and ask for others alongside it. Next step

The category needs load data The input to categorisation is the load profile: average, peak, seasonality and the origin of the wastewater. Without it the classification remains an estimate. Load profile Load profile Frequently asked questions

Load profile The nominal headcount is only one figure. Design needs the wastewater's load profile over time and by quality — and that differs by type of facility. What sizing can be based on

reszek.cim: The nominal headcount is only one figure
reszek.szoveg: The nominal headcount is only one figure For a larger system, the nominal headcount or bed count is not enough on its own. Design needs the wastewater's load profile over time and by quality is what is needed. The profile contains at least these: the average daily volume of water, the maximum daily and short-period hydraulic peak, the operating days, the seasonal variation and the origin of the wastewater. This is not bureaucracy. It shows whether the system can run stably under real operation — or only on average days. It differs by type of facility

Which figure is decisive? The same way of expressing capacity cannot serve a dwelling, a school, a restaurant and a plant alike. 01 A guesthouse, accommodation. The occupancy and the peak weekends determine the sizing situation — not the bed count. 02 School, institution. The daytime load window, the drop at weekends and the longer holidays. A strong daily rhythm with substantial periods of underload. 03 Campsite, holiday camp. The seasonal maximum and the near-zero load out of season. An extreme curve. 04 Restaurant, commercial kitchen. The kitchen's operating hours and the number of meals a day. Here the organic load can be the bottleneck, not the volume of water. 05 Plant, works. The shifts and the process water streams. The staff headcount applies only to the sanitary stream. Two separate loads

reszek.cim: They have to be measured separately and sized separately
reszek.szoveg: They have to be measured separately and sized separately Hydraulic — how much WATER arrives Average m³/day Maximum m³/day Hourly or per-shift peak, where relevant Read from the water meter; measured at an existing facility The unit's throughput capacity is the constraint Organic — how much MATTER has to be broken down BOD5, COD and suspended solids At a commercial kitchen or a plant it requires laboratory analysis It cannot be read off the water meter It can differ greatly at the same volume of water The basis for sizing the biological stage Data quality

reszek.cim: Four levels, and all of them matter
reszek.szoveg: Four levels, and all of them matter Where there is no reliable figure, do not estimate — mark the uncertainty and start gathering data. 01 Measured. Water meter data, laboratory results, operating log. This can be relied on. 02 Documented. An earlier drawing, permit or occupancy statement. Good, but whether it is current has to be checked. 03 Estimated. The owner's knowledge and experience. Enough for pre-screening, not for sizing. 04 Unknown. Not a failing but a task: measurement, sampling or expert data gathering follows from it. Next step

reszek.szoveg: After the profile comes the pre-treatment Once the load is assembled, the next question is whether anything is needed ahead of the biological stage — a grease trap, balancing, a pumping station. Capacity and project categories Pre-treatment and accessories Frequently asked questions

reszek.cim: What we are asked most often
reszek.szoveg: What we are asked most often We have no water consumption figures; the facility has not been built yet. For a new facility an estimate is needed: from the planned capacity, the operating pattern and data from comparable businesses. We mark the uncertainty separately in that case, and more headroom has to be built into the design. Is a laboratory analysis needed? For a purely domestic load, typically not a precondition. For a commercial kitchen, a significant grease load and any wastewater of process origin, yes — without it the sizing would rest on assumption. What is a load curve? How the load runs over time: how the daily volume of water varies across the week, the month and the year. It shows the spread around the average — and that is what determines how much headroom is needed.
Monitoring and operation Handover is not the end of the project but the start of a regulated operating process. And this has to be known as early as the choice of technology.

Handover is not the end At a larger treatment plant, handover is not the end of the project but the start of a the start of a regulated operating process. This has to be settled before the quote, because it affects the choice of technology too. The responsible operator has to be named, along with the frequency of checks, the content of the operating log, the sampling and laboratory duties, how alarms are handled and the service response time. The regulations do not treat this as optional either: the authority may check that the operating log is kept, that self-monitoring results conform, and that the discharge limits are observed — the detailed rules for sampling and analysis are set out in a separate decree. Who does what

Division of responsibility The on-site operator Daily and weekly visual checks Keeping the operating log Tracking flow and load First response and notification in the event of an alarm Keeping the sampling point accessible Managing consumables ÖkoTech and the laboratory Preventive maintenance and periodic inspection Parts replacement, mechanical repair Checking and setting the controller Resolving escalated faults Accredited laboratory: sampling and analysis Evaluating the results and reporting A regular feladatok

Daily, weekly, monthly, annual The exact schedule depends on the project and follows what the permit prescribes. The structure, however, is similar at every larger plant. 01 Napi or heti. Visual check, checking the state of the controller, an entry in the operating log, tracking the incoming flow. 02 Monthly. A more detailed inspection, checking the consumables, collating the load data. 03 At the frequency prescribed in the permit. Sampling and laboratory analysis, comparing the results with the discharge requirements. 04 Annual. A full inspection, preventive maintenance, parts replacement, collating the documentation and reporting. 05 Ad hoc. Alarms, overload, a deviation in water quality — these need an escalation procedure set out in advance. What has to be decided in advance

Before the quote, not after 01 Who the named responsible operator is, and with what competence 02 What training they receive, and when 03 Who covers for them during leave and holidays 04 What data is measured, and how often 05 Who takes the samples, and which laboratory analyses them 06 Who evaluates the results, and who they report to 07 What happens in the event of a fault — who is called, and within what time 08 Whether there is remote monitoring, and if so, who watches it 09 What service response time we undertake, and under what arrangement 10 Where and for how long the documentation is kept Next step

The permit sets it too The frequency and content of monitoring is partly prescribed by the permit. So the permitting route is worth looking at early too. Pre-treatment and accessories Permitting Frequently asked questions

reszek.cim: What we are asked most often
reszek.szoveg: What we are asked most often Does it need a qualified operator? The requirement depends on the project, and the permit may set it too. What is certain: a named person responsible is needed, with training, and the task is not a side activity. We agree the exact level of competence on the specific project. Is there remote monitoring? We are currently documenting the controller's capabilities and the remote monitoring option. On a specific project we will tell you what is available — precisely rather than in general terms. How quickly does a service engineer come out? We promise no specific response time here, because it is a contractual matter and depends on the arrangement. On a larger system this is exactly what is worth recording in the quote — ask, and we will agree it. What happens if it deviates from the discharge limit? An investigation of the cause follows: load, pre-treatment, the condition of the biology, a departure from the operating regime. The regulatory consequences are set by the permit and the legislation — which is why it matters that self-monitoring flags the deviation in good time.
Permitting Four branches by method of discharge, and one thing we do not promise: that the website will tell you which authority to approach.

reszek.cim: There is no single sequence of steps
reszek.szoveg: There is no single sequence of steps At a larger or community treatment plant the permitting route depends on the capacity, the origin of the wastewater, the receiving water, the method of discharge and the location . So it cannot be described with a single sequence of steps valid for every project — and anyone who promises otherwise is simplifying. What this page gives: a decision map of which project data, discipline drawings and experts are needed, and where the route branches. A correction

reszek.cim: The naming of the competent authority is out of date
reszek.szoveg: The naming of the competent authority is out of date Our earlier material directed enquirers to an inspectorate under an organisational name that no longer exists. We have not carried that over to this page. The name of the competent water and water-protection authority and the procedural regime change from time to time. So here we deliberately name no specific organisation: it has to be checked from a current source when the project starts, and that is how we proceed too. Four branches

reszek.cim: The method of discharge determines the route
reszek.szoveg: The method of discharge determines the route 01 Disposal into the soil, into the geological medium. The soil, the groundwater and the area's sensitivity classification are decisive. Here the plot suitability questions become permitting questions directly. 02 Discharge to a surface receiving water. It requires a water permit and compliance with the discharge requirements. The state of the receiving water and the requirements set for it are decisive. 03 Into a mains sewer or a shared works system. Where this arises at all, the utility's conditions and any pre-treatment requirement are decisive. 04 Putting the treated water to further use. A separate route with its own water quality, monitoring and permitting conditions. It cannot be treated as a simple variant of on-site disposal. What data and documents are needed

reszek.cim: The elements of the permitting package
reszek.szoveg: The elements of the permitting package The specific requirements are set by the permit and the situation of the receiving water. This list shows the typical elements. 01 Project capacity in PE and in m³/day 02 The origin and character of the wastewater, with laboratory data where needed 03 Description of the technology 04 Load data — average, peak, seasonality 05 A site plan and a description of the water streams 06 The method and place of discharge or disposal 07 Monitoring plan 08 Operating plan and the responsible operator 09 The pre-treatment applied 10 Documentation prepared by a qualified designer On the earlier permit examples

Why they are not guides We hold permit documents belonging to earlier projects. They can be useful as examples — they show what data such a procedure contained — but as dated case studies, not as today's procedural guide. A permit from a few years ago does not prove that a permit would be granted automatically today, and it does not describe today's procedure. So when we show one, we always show it with its date and this note. Next step

reszek.cim: What we are asked most often
reszek.szoveg: What we are asked most often Do you handle the permitting? Exactly what we undertake of the permitting and what an external qualified designer prepares, we agree project by project — and we are recording that internal division of responsibility right now. What we certainly provide: the technology description and the unit's documentation. How long does permitting take? We give no general answer, because it depends on the type of procedure, the receiving water and the authority's handling. What is worth knowing: requests for missing documents are the commonest loss of time, and that depends largely on the quality of the preparation. Which authority has to be approached? Pre-treatment and accessories The biological reactor is only one element of the whole system. What goes before and after it is often the condition of stable operation — but none of it is automatic.

reszek.cim: The reactor is only one element
reszek.szoveg: The reactor is only one element On a larger or more complex project, the biological treatment unit before and after further technical elements may be needed for stable operation. These are not extras; often they are conditions of operation. It matters, though, that none of them is an automatic accessory. Each has to be judged from the origin, composition, temperature and load of the wastewater — from project data, not from a template. What PROTECTS the biological stage

Inlet side Without these the biology can be damaged, blocked, or lose its efficiency. 01 Mechanical pre-treatment, screen. Retaining the coarser solids, where the incoming wastewater warrants it. 02 Grease separator or grease trap. For a large volume of kitchen wastewater. Grease forms a film on the surface and impairs oxygen transfer — but whether one is needed has to be derived from the particular kitchen, not from a general rule. 03 Grit or sediment separation. Depending on the project, where the incoming wastewater warrants it. 04 Oil and hydrocarbon separation. Only where the activity makes it relevant — not a general accessory. 05 Balancing tank. Where the peaks swing widely. It spreads a large volume arriving suddenly over time, so the biological stage receives a steadier load. What solves the hydraulics

reszek.cim: And what stands on the outlet side
reszek.szoveg: And what stands on the outlet side 01 Wastewater pumping station. Where the pipe levels are unfavourable, or where several incoming branches arrive at different levels. 02 Emergency or reserve volume. Where operational reliability warrants it — for instance where an outage would have serious consequences. 03 Treated water tank. If the outlet water is put to use, or if disposal is spread over time. 04 Post-treatment or disinfection. If the receiving water or the intended use requires it. This is already a discharge question. 05 Sampling point. A precondition of monitoring — its position has to be fixed at the design stage, not solved afterwards. 06 Odour control and ventilation. Where the location of the installation warrants it. 07 Automation and alarms. Fault and level indication — on a larger system this is not an extra. For every element

Four possible ratings How we rate them Required — a condition of operation Required conditionally — in given circumstances Not warranted — not needed on this project Laboratory or design analysis is needed to decide What this follows from The origin and composition of the wastewater The daily and peak load The existing pre-treatment, if any The receiving water and the discharge requirement The location and circumstances of the installation Next step

And who will watch it? The sampling point, the alarms and the control system are already questions of operation — and they have to be settled before the quote, not at handover. Load profile Monitoring and operation Frequently asked questions

reszek.cim: What we are asked most often
reszek.szoveg: What we are asked most often Does every restaurant need a grease trap? We do not assert it in general. The regulations prescribe pre-treatment for the wastewater of certain activities, and a heavy kitchen grease load is indeed a typical reason — but whether one is needed in a given business, and in what size, has to be derived from how the kitchen operates and from measurements. What is a balancing tank? A volume acting as a buffer ahead of the biological stage. If a large volume of water arrives in a short time — after an event, for instance — it spreads it over time, so the biology takes no sudden shock. Can an accessory be retrofitted? In many cases yes, but typically at greater cost and difficulty than at the design stage. This is especially true of the sampling point and the balancing tank — both worth designing in from the start.
Technical consultation The aim is that both parties hold the necessary basic data before the consultation — so the conversation is about decisions, not about gathering data.

Not a quotation request form This page closes the preliminary technical qualification of a larger project; it is not a name–telephone–message box. The aim is that before the consultation both parties have the necessary basic data. That way our specialist receives not a raw enquiry of the „price for a 200-bed hotel please” kind but a structured decision situation — and you are not told back that „this needs more data”. What the brief records

Five groups of data 01 Project identification. Type of facility, project owner or operator, location, project stage, intended commissioning date, new or existing system. 02 Load. Nominal headcount or bed count, average daily occupancy, peak occupancy, average and maximum m³/day, operating days, seasonal curve, shifts, expansion plans. 03 The character of the wastewater. Purely domestic, commercial kitchen, process or mixed; existing laboratory results; existing pre-treatment. 04 Plot and discharge. Available area, pipe levels, soil and groundwater, receiving water, water disposal, existing network. 05 Project readiness and operation. Existing drawings, permitting status, monitoring requirements, the responsible operator, maintenance model, service expectations, procurement process. What it returns

The output of the brief What you get Project category — which route it falls into Completeness of the data: what is in place, what is missing A list of the investigations required Which expert it is worth involving An agenda for the consultation The next person responsible and the next step Ezt not kapja An automatic specific price A price band for an unsettled project scope A guaranteed capacity from incomplete data Automatic industrial sizing without laboratory data A promise that it can be permitted A final product model The possible outcomes

Five outcomes, five routes 01 Standard domestic project. The data is sufficient and the load is domestic in character. Design can proceed. 02 Modular community system. The load exceeds the standalone category but can be built from known elements. 03 Large-plant design. A purpose-built high-capacity system, with a qualified designer. 04 Special or industrial analysis. Non-domestic wastewater. Sampling and a feasibility study follow, not a capacity estimate. 05 Further data gathering is needed. The constraint is not the project but the information. The brief says which figure, and from where.

What is worth attaching Attach what you have: a site plan, mechanical drawings, a consumption series, an earlier drawing or permit, laboratory results, and — if you already have one — an existing quote. With these we reach a technical direction considerably faster, and the consultation can be about decisions rather than about gathering data. We set out how we handle data on the contact page; we use the documents you attach solely to answer your enquiry. In the meantime

reszek.szoveg: What we are asked most often Why do I not get a price straight away? Because on a larger system a price quoted from capacity or headcount would mislead. The project cost is determined together by the system architecture, the pre-treatment, the earthworks, the control system, the water disposal, the design and the operation. The emptying history, additive use and state of the field of a holiday-home system running for years prove or refute those claims directly. Where there is no such data, the claim cannot appear in a strong form either. That is the order of things — not the other way round. Next step

reszek.cim: What we are asked most often
reszek.szoveg: What we are asked most often Why are there not many case studies here? Because we show only those where a septic tank system is actually running and where the data needed for a decision is available too. We are working on gathering them — better fewer but usable cases than many photographs without data. Can I speak to an existing owner? That depends on the customer's consent, but in several cases it can be arranged. The owner of a system running for years can usually speak more precisely about emptying and daily life with it than any data sheet.
Drainage field and space required The question is not whether the tank fits — but whether the field fits. Most of the breakdown happens there, so its size is decisive. The central point

reszek.cim: The field is part of the system, not an accessory
reszek.szoveg: The field is part of the system, not an accessory A septic tank system is not the tank put in the ground but a system working together with a properly built drainage field. The tank is the first, mechanical and anaerobic stage of treatment; the second stage takes place in the field. From this follows the most important practical rule: most of the breakdown happens in the drainage field, so its proper size is of decisive importance. The question is not whether the tank fits — but whether the field fits. What the area required depends on

Five factors together So no fixed square-metres-per-person rule can be given: a change in a single factor can multiply the area required. 01 The MEASURED infiltration capacity of the soil. Not the name of the soil but the result of the percolation test. This is the most powerful factor. 02 A napi szennyvolume of water. It follows from the household's load. A greater load needs a proportionally larger field. 03 A groundwater. The field has to work above the groundwater, in an aerated layer — at the seasonal maximum too. 04 The design of the field. A perforated drain, an infiltration chamber or another distribution element works with a different area requirement. 05 The manufacturer's sizing rule. The requirement belonging to the particular product system, which ties the above together. Over the field

reszek.cim: What may be done, and what may not
reszek.szoveg: What may be done, and what may not Typically permitted Grass and shallow-rooted planting Occasional foot traffic Open, maintained green space Knowing and marking the line of the field It does not javasolt or tiltott Paving, concreting, compaction Planting deep-rooted trees and shrubs Directing rainwater onto it — the field takes an extra load Placing a structure over the field or immediately beside it Breaking into the area without knowing the line of the distribution pipes Site plan

reszek.cim: What to mark for the area check
reszek.szoveg: What to mark for the area check A hand-drawn sketch to scale is acceptable. 01 The outline of the house and where the wastewater pipe leaves it 02 The intended position of the septic tank 03 The area intended for the drainage field 04 The position of the well or wells — including those on neighbouring plots 05 The driveway, parking, paved surfaces 06 The line of known utilities 07 Large trees and planting to be kept 08 The direction of the ground slope 09 Structures planned for later — this is what is most often left out Next step

Sizing the field needs measurement The input to sizing the drainage field is the measured infiltration capacity of the soil. Without it every size is an estimate — and putting right a badly sized field is substantial work. Plot suitability Percolation test Frequently asked questions

reszek.cim: What we are asked most often
reszek.szoveg: What we are asked most often How many square metres are needed? We deliberately give no figure for this, because without the measured infiltration capacity of the soil it would rest on nothing. The same household needs a much smaller area on one soil and several times that on another. The measurement is the input. Can a parking area be built over the field? Our current material mentions such a possibility with adequate earth cover, but it has to be traced back to a specific product type and layer build-up. Until that is documented we do not promise it — ask on the specific project. What happens if the field clogs? The water does not percolate away fast enough, it backs up, damp can appear at the surface, and the treatment efficiency falls. The causes can include compaction, overloading, rainwater discharged into it, and emptying left undone. Putting it right typically means partly or wholly rebuilding the field. Can the field be extended later? In principle yes, if there is somewhere for it. So it is worth allowing for extension at the design stage — and not building on the area beside it.
Emptying and maintenance That it needs no electricity does not mean it needs no attention. None of the tasks is large — but every one of them recurs.

No electricity ≠ no maintenance That the system needs no electricity does not mean it needs no attention. The bottom sludge and scum layer accumulating in the septic tank have to be removed periodically, and the condition of the filter and the drainage field has to be checked. To this is added the bacterial additive dosing regularly, which is a substantial difference from an active biological system — there the culture is self-sustaining. This is a recurring task and a consumables cost. Neither is a great burden, but both recur. Anyone who knows this in advance will not be disappointed. Emptying

reszek.cim: Why, when and on what basis
reszek.szoveg: Why, when and on what basis 01 Why. Anaerobic breakdown does not make the solids disappear. What remains accumulates at the bottom and over time narrows the tank, burdening the filter and the drainage field. 02 On what basis. The sludge level is what governs, not the calendar. The fullness of the tank has to be checked — a calendar cycle is only a rough guide. 03 What affects it. The size of the tank, the number of users, the intensity of use and the amount of sludge accumulated. At a rarely used holiday home it is considerably less frequent than at a permanently occupied house. 04 Documentation. The regulations also require documents relating to the lawful disposal of the waste produced to be retained. So it is worth keeping the emptying receipts. Who does what

Division of responsibility The owner's responsibility Checking the sludge level periodically Checking the condition of the filter and cleaning it as needed Dosing the bacterial additive regularly Protecting the area over the drainage field Arranging the emptying and keeping the receipts Reporting odour, damp or backing up Contractor or specialist Carrying out the emptying — a licensed contractor Lawful disposal of the waste, with proof Investigating odour, backing up or silting Professional assessment of the drainage field's condition Restoration in the event of a fault or saturation Advice on restarting after a longer gap Warning signs

When is a specialist needed? Every one of these suggests something is not working as designed — and the sooner it comes to light, the simpler it is to deal with. 01 A persistent smell near the tank or the field 02 Damp or standing water over the drainage field 03 Backing up in the house — a slow drain, gurgling 04 The tank fills faster than expected 05 The filter clogs frequently 06 Unusually lush growth over the field — it can be a sign of saturation Next step
